full_judgment:
the rest of 2.19 acres to his wife Amisa Khatun and son. Abdul Mannan. Asiran Khatun is defendant No. 23 Am isa Khatun and son, Abdul Manna. Asiran Khatun is defendant No. 23 Amisa Khatun and Abdul Mannan then possessed their land and transferred by various transaction: to the answering defendants. Further case of the defendants are that after purchase they got their names mutated paid rent and possessed the land for more than 12 years and perfected their title by adverse possession. Said defendants also claimed that the plaintiffs are not related either to Debicharan Mondal or Kaichu Barmani and hence, are not co-sharers in the suit land. Therefore, the simple suit for partition in the absence of a declaration of title is not maintainable. 

 4. On the pleadings, issues regarding maintainability of the suit, defect of parties, title and/or possession of the 'plaintiffs of the suit land etc. were framed plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses while defendants examined 7 witnesses. plaintiffs documents were marked Exhibit. I and 2 (series) while those of the defendants marked as exhibit. Ka to Nio (I) series. 

 5. Trial Court though found the plaintiffs have got right, title and possession in the suit land and all other issues in favour of the plaintiffs but 'dismissed the suit only on the ground that the entire land of C.S. Khatian 86 was not brought into hotchpot. 

 7. Mr: Md. Zahidul Bari, learned Advocate for the petitioners assails the decree firstly on the ground that the court of appeal erred in law in decreeing the suit when plaintiffs failed to prove that they are co-share in the suit land. By reading section 88 of Mullas Principles of Hundu Law, he submits that under the Hindu Law the plaintiffs even if be conceded to be heirs of Rupchan and /or Debicharan have no right to inherit to the suit land as they are excluded from inheritance as female heirs. he also submits that the courts below erred in law in finding the plaintiffs as the lawfully heirs of Rupchand and/or Debicharan in the absence of any lawful evidence. Lastly, he submits that the said defendants having been in possession for more then 30 years on payment of rent, they have perfected their title at least by adverse possession against the plaintiffs. 

 8. Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mondal, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs opposite party No. l and 2 on the other hand submits that when the original title documents of Asiran Nessa, Am isa Khatun and Abdul Mannan were concurrently found by the courts below as collusive, forged, fraudulent and void. The defendants cannot resist the plaintiffs from getting the decree for partition when they are proved to be daughters and sisters of the original rightful owner Rupchand and Debicharan respectively. He further submits that record of rights in respect of the suit land was prepared even after Bangladesh in the name of Debicharan and others including those who purchased from Debicharan and as such, the contesting defendants cannot claim any land was exclusively recorded in their names or they possessed exclusively any land. When they claim to have entered into possession through attorney, they cannot claim now adverse possession against the principals. He further submits that both the courts below have concurrently found that the plaintiffs are daughters left by original owner Rupchand and sisters Debicharan and accordingly in the absence of any other heirs they were rightly found to have inherited. the rest of the suit land He also cites the case of Lai Meah. Vs. Haji Md. Ibrahim Meah and ors (1976) 28 DLR (AD) 61 to submits that the record of rights is not a document of title. 

 9. We have perused the record and heard the learned Advocates at length. As stated above, the suit land measuring 7.62 acres originally belonged to Rupchand Mondal and C. S. record of rights was so prepared in his name. According to the plaintiffs Rupchand died leaving a wife Kaichu Bramani and son Debicharan and two daughters, the plaintiff, which the contesting defendants denied and claimed that the plaintiffs were not daughters of Rupchand. It is also not disputed that during the lifetime. Debicharan transferred 3.24 acres of land. He died leaving a mother and the plaintiffs according to the plaint case but only the mother as per the defence case. As daughters and / or sisters, plaintiffs claimed rest of the entire suit land measuring 4.38 acres. It appears that the trial court found the deeds on which the fate of the defendants rests Exhibit. 'C' and 'F' are collusive, without consideration and void. Then, it found the plaintiffs have right, title and possession in the suit land as heirs. The suit also does not suffer from any defect of parties. Even after deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs trial court held, in the absence of bringing entire land of C. S. Khatian 86 into hotchpot suit for partition is not maintainable. Trial Court accordingly dismissed the suit. Appellate Court affirmed the findings of the trial Court and reversed the conclusion of the trial court regarding hotchpot on the view that entire land of C. S. Khatian 86 was clearly sught for partition. We have also perused the C. S. Khatian and find that the appellate Court has rightly reversed the conclusion of the trial court. First, no issue was raised in the suit nor Mr. Md. Zahidul Bari . did advance any submission thereon. 

 11. Now, whether as sisters they could inherit lawfully the estate left by their brother Debicharan. Section 25 of Mullas Principles of Hindu Law says according to the Bengal School there are only five females who can succeed as heirs to a male, namely 1. Widow 2. Daughter, 3. Mother 4. Fathers mother and 5. Fathers Fathers mother. Three more were added to the list by the Hindu Lai' v of inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, namely, the sons daughter, daughters daughter and sister. Section 88 of the same Book provides the order of succession among Sapindas. There is no mention of sister. Absence of sister there only to indicate the heirs in whose presence, a sister is excluded. Section 88.does not take away the right of a sister as recognized under section 25. Under section 25 sisters are entitled to inherit the estate of her 

 brother of Debicharan. Therefore, the court of appeal below did not commit any error in affirming the finding of the trial court that the plaintiffs are lawfully entitled to the land left by their brother Debicharan and when they acquired the land by inheritances, they are definitely entitled to sue for partition. 

 12. Lastly, let us see Whether the possession of the contesting defendants could be that of an adverse possession. Appellate Court has affirmed the finding that the plaintiffs have possession of the suit land. We have also perused the record and found that the decision does not suffer from any infirmity' or illegality. Though Mr. Zahidul Bari failed to point out any material evidence either not read or misread in coming such finding on possession. When the plaintiffs are fond to be in possession, even if in a portion of the suit land they are entitled to maintain their suit even for simple partition against the co-sharers namely who acquired the land from Bebicharan and their successors. On the other hand, the contesting defendants claimed to have entered into the land by way of successive purchase. It is on record defendant No. 23 Asiran Nessa got the land from her husband Faraz Ali Mondal who transferred as an attorney of Debicharan. Similarly, Nur Ali Mondal transferred '/2 of the rest of the land to his wife and son Abdul Manan, Defendant failed to produce their so-called power of attorney of Faraz Ali Mondal and Nur Ali Mondal. The Courts below have found the deeds of transfer by Faraz Ali Mondal and Nur Ali Mondal to their respect wives dated 25.4.1959 collusive, without consideration and void. So the possession of Asiran Nessa, defendant No. 23 cannot be deemed to be adverse to the plaintiffs since the possession of an attorney would be at best of a Manager on behalf of the principal. Similarly, the possession of other defendants having entered lawfully cannot convert into hostitle or adverse. We could not find any material on record which will suggest that the defendant possessed any land exclusively and adversely against the plaintiffs. In the absence of the animus, mere possession on payment of rent does not turn such possession into adverse or hostitle.

parties:
Kajemuddin Miah (Md) ------ Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh and other ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
The petitioner and his grand-parents were originally residents of Mouza Rohai Ramnagar, PS Sadarpur District Faridpur. His grandfather Babar Ali Sheikh along with others had lands and homesteads in Mouza Rabairamnagar, PS Bhanga (now Sadarpur), District Faridpur. Due to erosion of the river Padma the lands and homestead of the petitioner and other co-villagers were diluviated and went under water in 1947. So they shifted their residence and settled in Mouza Charbhadrason, Kallyanpur, etc. within the district of Faridpur in 1948. When the lands appeared the petitioner and other co-villagers took settlement from the Government and the usufruct thereof. Due to subsequent erosion the petitioner and co-villagers Shifted their homestead to Jhaukanda, Char Kurulla,Char Deaobhet, Char Hatni, Partuil, etc. within the Dohar Police Station in the district of Dhaka in 1956 and took lands from the old tenants by purchase and took permanent settlement from the Government and have been residing there with their families and became inhabitants of Dohar Police Station in the district of Dhaka. Due to erosion of the river Padma they shifted their residence in the interior side of the Dohar Police Station in 1991 and the petitioner purchased 6.14 acres of land from the recorded tenants Nuni Gopal Gopini and others on 24-1-1977 appertaining to SA Khatian Nos. 144, 206, 380 of Plot No. 332, 832 and 396 Mouza Kartickpur within PS Dohar, district Dhaka. The petitioner filed a Civil suit being Title Suit No. 19 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge Dohar, Dhaka against Nuni Gopal Gopini and others for specific performance of Contract and the said suit was decreed in favour of the petitioner on 3-2-1987 and in execution of the decree in Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1987 the petitioner got the deed registered through Civil Court being Deed No. 2419 dated 16-11-1991. The aforesaid lands of the petitioner was again diluviated and went under the water of river Padma in 1992. The lands of the petitioner and other co- villagers of Mouza Charbhadrason, PS Char Bhadrason District Faridpur were diluviated and went under water due to erosion of the river Padma and subsequently appeared and reformed in situ and the petitioner and other co-villagers took settlement from the Government and paid rents, Thereafter again the lands was diluviated and went under water in 1991. This way the petitioner was affected by diluvion of his lands 11 times and lastly, in 1991-1992 when the aforesaid mentioned land was diluviated in the district of Faridpur and in Dohar PS District Dhaka. 

 3. The petitioner has given a short background of the law relating to diluvion land alluvion of lands By the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No. XXVIII of 1951) the rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the said land were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant could hold. No substantial charge with regard to this law as to accretion or reformation in situ was brought about by this enactment excepting the law of accretion (which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825) was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenant's title in respect of such land, similar to those contained in section 86(A) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for abatement of rent on account of diluvion and re-entry into lands which re-appear, Time to time the law relating to the tenant's fight on his diluviated land were passed. On 13-7-1994 the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act, 1994 (Act No. 15 of 1994) was promulgated substituting in place of the old section 86 with regard to abatement of rent on account of diluvion and determination of right in land reappearing on account of alluvion. By the said Act the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successor-in-interest would subsist in the lands of a holding or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appeared in situ within thirty years of their loss instead of 20 years. The respondent No. 1 by the impugned order as contained in letter No ML/S-9-24/94-764/1(40) dated 29-11-1994 issued to all the Deputy Commissioners of the districts containing guidelines for implementation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994 and directing them to take necessary steps for processing the diluvion and reformation of land. By the said impugned order it was directed that all land already diluviated and alluviated shall vest in the Government as the said Act dated 13th July, 1994 was prospective and not retrospective. The petitioner is aggrieved by the circular because it is not in accordance with the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act of 1994 and by the said circular his subsisting right on the lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 in the district of Faridpur and in Dohar Police Station, District Dhaka has been taken away, and is therefore, constrained to file this writ petition challenging the validity of the impugned order (Annexure 'D'). 

 4. The question before us is, whether the petitioners right on his lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 subsists under the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act, 1994. It may be convenient to quote the relevant portion of the laws passed at different times with regard to the abatement of rent, right, title and interest of the owner on diluvion and alluvion of his land. By the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent was abated and the right, title and interest of the owner to diluvion subsisted for 20 years under section 86 of the said Act which reads as follows: 

 Abatement of rent on account of diluvion and extinguishment of right, title and interest of the tenant thereto-86(1) if the lands of a holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent of the holding shall, on application made by the tenant in the prescribed form to the Revenue-Officer, be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue-Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the rule made in his behalf by the Provincial Government. 

 2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successor-in-interest shall subsist in such lands or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion, not exceeding twenty years, whether partly before and partly after or wholly after the commencement of this Order and the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall have the right to immediate re-possession on the re-appearance of such lands or portion thereof within twenty years of their loss by diluvion, and be liable to pay such fair and equitable rent in respect thereof as may be settled by the Revenue-Officer: 

 Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was amended by President's Order No.135 of 1972. The rent abated. The right, title and interest of tenant extinguished whether loss was due to diluvion before or after commencement of said order. The relevant portion of the Bangladesh State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (4th Amendment) Order 1972 President's Order No. 135 of 1972. President Order No. 135 of 1972 by Article 2 provided as follows: 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. 

 6. Lastly, by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act 1994 (Act XV of 1994) section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was again amended whereby the rent abated The right, title and interest of the owner subsists for 30 years. It provided for the right of Collector to possess the land immediately upon reappearance and publication of notice, survey, map and allotment to tenant, the amendment of section 86 by Act XV of 1994 reads as follows: 

 "86 Abatement of rent on account of diluvion and determination of right in land re-appeared on account of alluvion (I) If the lands of a holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent or the land development tax of holding shall, on application or intimation made by the tenant in the prescribed form to the Revenue Officer, be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the Rule made in this behalf by the Government and the act of such loss by diluvion shall be recorded in accordance with such rules, which shall be treated as proof of title to the lands when the same re-appear in situ. 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successor-in-interest shall subsist in the lands of a holding or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appear in situ within thirty years of their loss." 

 (3) Notwithstanding the right, title and interest under sub-section (2), the right to immediate possession of the lands re-appeared shall first be exercised by the Collector, either on his own motion or on intimation made in writing by the tenant or his successors-in-interest whose land was so lost or by any other person. 

 7. The petitioner's case is that by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1994 (Act XV of 1995) the right, title and interest in his land lost by diluvion in 1991 and 1992 has been restored and on its re-appearance he is entitled to get its allotment subject to ceiling imposed by the Act as tenant of the land. If the impugned order is not interfered with his right of ownership which has been restored by the Act, 1994 will be taken away. It is submitted that the respondent has misconstrued both the provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 and the Act of 1994 which amended section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950. The respondent has illegally notified that the State Acquisition and Tenancy Amendment Act, 1994 is effective from 13th July, 1994 that the right, title and interest of all lands which had diluviated or alluviated prior to that date i.e. 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the said Act of 1994 will be applicable only to dilluvion and alluvion of land after 13th July, 1994 i.e. the Act is retrospective and not re-prospective. It may be convenient to quote the impugned order Annexure 'D' to see whether it has been passed in accordance with law. 

 8. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents has defended the impugned order as being in accordance with law. He argued that the Act of 1994 was not retrospective as was specifically provided in President's Order 135 of 1972. Because if was not made re-Prospective the lands which had diluviated and alluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 would be recorded in Khas Khatian. He particularly relied on the amendment made to section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 by which the right, title and interest of the land vested in the Government. He argued since the right, title and interest of the tenant extinguished by diluvion under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest vested with the Government. As such, the right of the Government could not be substituted under sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended by Act (XV of 1994,) because it was not given retrospective effect. The right, title and interest in land which vested in the Government on diluvion by amendment of the Act under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 was not taken away, The learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that the land vested absolutely in the Government at point of diluvion under the President's Order 1972. In this connection we may refer to the amendment made by the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 in respect of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 with regard to abatement of rent by diluvion and extinguishment of right, title and interest of the tenant thereto. Sub-section (2) of Ordinance 2 of the Order relates to the extinguishment of the right, title and interest of the tenant by diluvion. This sub-section does not say that on diluvion the tenant's right, title and interest shall vest in the government, Clause 3 of Article 2 of the said Order says about vesting in the Government and this clause (3) says all lands lost by diluvion under sub-section (2) which re-appeared before the date of commencement of the said order but in respect of which the right of the tenant whose land was lost on his successors-in-interest to re- possession was not recognised or declared by a competent authority or court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal (our emphasis) It is clear from this clause 3 that although by clause 2 of the article the right, title and interest of the tenant is extinguished on diluvion the right, title and interest will vest in the Government in respect of such diluviated land on its re-appearance. Therefore, we are not in agreement with the statement made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the diluviated land vest absolutely in the Government at the point of diluvion. The Government can claim title and interest in the land diluviated after re-appearance. It cannot claim vesting under the said order while the land remains diliuviated By sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by Act XV of 1994 the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successors-in-interest shall subsist in the lands of a holding on operation thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appear in situ within thirty years of their loss It would only follow that the land which were in diluvion prior to 13th July, 1994 the right of the original tenant or his successors in those lands would continue if the land re-appear in situ within 30 years. The Government can only claim such of these lands in diluvion which had re-appeared prior to 13th July, 1994 under the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 but cannot claim such right in respect of lands which is still is diluvion. Therefore, the impugned order in respect of land which re-appeared (alluviated) prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands. We find that the impugned order 'Annexure D' to the extent giving a direction that all lands diluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands in diluvion to be illegal and without lawful authority.

parties:
Shamsun Nahar Begum ------ Appellant
Vs.
Salauddin Ahmed and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is against the judgment and order dated 9-7-95 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 3744 of 1995 affirming the judgment and order dated 20-5-95 passed by the Assistant Judge. 1st Court, Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 60 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC allowing the said Misc. Case and setting aside the ex parte decree dated 25-4-85 and restoring original Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 to its file and number. 

 2. The plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. Against that ex parte judgment and decree defendant respondent filed on 25-9-91 Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff by suppression of all notices obtained the ex parte decree on 25-4-85, which he came to know by filing information slip on 23-4-91 through an Advocate, Shunil Ranjan Biswas; that thereafter by obtaining necessary papers he filed the case and that no summons was served upon him and the report of the serving peon is false. 

 3. Plaintiff appellant contested the Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that after taking the entire proposed money the agreement for sale was executed on 14-2-70 and possession was handed over along with the lease deed of the Housing Estate and all other documents; that thereafter another agreement was executed on 8-10-77; that the plaintiff was residing in the said house all through; that notice was served in the original suit as well as at the time of registration of the document; that the defendant had full knowledge about the construction of the building and the living of the tenants; that the alleged knowledge dated 23-4-91 is absolutely false and the application is liable, to be dismissed; that the information slip stands in the name of one Shahabuddin Ahmed and not in the name of defendant No. 1. Plaintiff further asserted that the plaintiff's name has been duly mutated in the office of the Housing Estate, Ministry of Works, Municipality, WASA, WAPDA, Titas Gas, etc. and due notices were served upon defendant No. 1 for those mutation proceedings. The defendant had full prior knowledge of the decree and the pucca construction and, as such, the Miscellaneous case that was filed long after six years without any application for condemnation of delay is liable to be dismissed.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 76 of 1986.
parties:
Kala Miah ------ Appellant
vs
Gopal Chandra Paul and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 63 of 1985. By the impugned judgment dated 30-6-1986 the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. 

 2. The short fact leading to this appeal is, that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 63 of 1985 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur impleading the respondents as defendants praying for declaration of title by adverse possession in respect of the suit land described in schedule to the plaint and for declaration that the judgment and decree passed on 19-2-1985 and 25-2-1985 respectively by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 of the Court of the Munsif, Upazila, Hajigonj (Original Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 of the Second Court of Munsif, Chandpur) instituted by defendant No. 3 are fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff asserted in the plaint that the suit land originally belonged to one Madhab Chandra Paul, who died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Horo Kumar Paul, Chandra Kumar Paul, Kali Kumar Paul and Raj Mohan Paul and each son inherited 4 annas share out of the suit jote. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and they left for India before partition. The plaintiff also asserted that Chandra Kumar Paul gifted his 1/4/- annas share to his wife Marani Paul who being owner thereof sold the same to the plaintiff on payment of Taka 2,000.00 by executing a bainapatra on 4-2-1959 in favour of the plaintiff. According to the plaintiff Dag No. 830 has been wrongly endorsed as Dag No. 833 in the bainapatra. The plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since his purchase. It has been further asserted that there was a rent suit bearing No. 292 of 1973 in the Court of the Munsif, Chandpur in which there was a compromise by the plaintiff with one Prasanna. Since purchase the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land for more then 12 years. The plaintiff further asserted that after the liberation the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 came to Bangladesh and joined with the plaintiff’s enemy and when the plaintiff asked the defendant No. 2 on 31-10-1981 to execute and register a kabala deed in his favour, the defendant No. 2 flatly refused. The defendant Nos. 3-6 filed a petition under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 20-5-1982 in Title Suit No. 564 of 1981, which was filed by the plaintiff when the plaintiff learned about the alleged sale deed of the defendants and about the decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1977 and hence filed the present suit. 

 3. Before the trial Court the defendant No. 3 entered appearance and contested the-suit by filing a written statement. Having denied all the averments made in the plaint the contesting defendant contended that the suit land originally belonged to Madhab Chandra, who died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Hore Kumar Paul, Chandra Kumar Paul, Kali Kumar Paul and Raj Kumar Paul. According to this defendant, Chandra Kumar Paul sold 0.80½ decimals of land for Taka 3,000.00 to this defendant No. 3 on the basis of bainapatra and delivered possession to this defendant. This defendant further alleged that as Chandra Mohan did not execute and register the sale deed on the basis of the bainapatra and accordingly, after the death of Chandra Mohan, this defendant No. 3 filed Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 against the sons of Chandra Mohan and others in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Chandpur which on transfer was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 20 of 1983. The said suit was dismissed by the trial Court against which the present defendant No.3 as appellant filed Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 and the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal. The defendant also asserted that the present plaintiff filed an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for adding him as a party in the said Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 which was rejected by the trial Court against which the plaintiff did not move any higher forum. This contesting defendant clearly asserted that the plaintiff has obtained a false and forged bainapatra in the name of Maroni Paul, who was not the wife of Chandra Kumar Paul and the alleged bainapatra dated 4-2-1959 is false and forged. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 564 of 1981 in the 2nd Court of the Munsif, Chandpur which on transfer to the Court of Munsif, Hajigonj was renumbered as Title Suit No. 298 of 1983 and subsequently on the prayer of the plaintiff this suit was withdrawn. The defendant asserted that the plaintiff has filed this suit on the same cause of action which is bad in law. This defendant further asserted that one Prasanna Kumar Paul and the present plaintiff in collusion with one another filed Title Execution Case No. 32 of 1972 which was beyond the knowledge of this defendant. It has been further asserted that in Title Suit No. 292 of 1973 no summons was served upon Gopal Chandra Paul and Chinta Haran Paul, who are the sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and solenama filed in that suit is collusive and void. Accordingly, this defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 5. Mr. Md Nurul Mostafa, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that the trial Court misconstrued the bainapatra Ext. 1 and committed an error in holding that the bainapatra has not been written at the instance of the executants Marani Paul. The learned Advocate submits that the learned Subordinate Judge mis-read the evidence of PW 4 and omitted to consider the admission of PW 1 made in his evidence that there is a homestead on the suit land which fits in with the plaintiff’s case. The learned Advocate also contends that since defendant Nos. 1-2, who are sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and Maroni Paul did not contest the suit to deny the fact of acquisition of title by their mother Marani Paul, on the basis of gift from Chandra Kumar Paul and also the execution of the bainapatra by her in favour of the plaintiff, the suit should have been decreed. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that acquisition of title by Marani Paul on the basis of oral gift from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul is valid in law. The learned Advocate submits that since donor and the donee both belong to Hindu community, provision of Hindu Law being their personal law shall prevail over the provision of the Transfer of Property Act and the oral gift is therefore valid to confer title on Marani Paul. 

 6. Mr. Mokbul Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff- respondent, on the other hand, supports the decision of the trial Court and submits that Marani did not acquire any title on the basis of oral gift from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul and therefore she had no authority to transfer the property on the basis of the agreement in favour of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate submits that for effecting a gift for immovable property by a Hindu the same may only be made by an instrument which must be a registered one and no oral gift is permissible. The learned Advocate referred to section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act and submits that for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses. The learned Advocate also submits that the bainapatra Ext. 1 is a forged and collusive document. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff filed the suit claiming declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession but in his evidence the plaintiff did not utter a single word about possession and he was not also supported by PW 2. On the other hand, the learned Advocate contends that PW 3 and 4 supports the possession of defendant No. 3 in the suit land. 

 12. Having considered the submissions of both the learned Advocates we hold that in the absence of a registered instrument a gift by a person belonging to Hindu community and governed under the Dayabhaga School of Hindu law is not valid in view of the provision of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. In view of this legal position Marani Paul did not acquire any title in the suit land on the basis of alleged oral gift and she was not competent to make any transfer of the same in any manner whatsoever including by a bainapatra as in the case before us. 

 13. The plaintiff asserted that Marani Paul executed a bainapatra on 4-2-1959 in his favour on receipt of Taka 2,000.00. To prove his case as regards execution of the bainapatra which has been marked Ext. 1, the plaintiff as PW deposed that one Jogendra Chandra Paul wrote the bainapatra. Bainaparra Ext. 1 shows that one Nagendra Chandra Paul was the scribe of the bainapatra. This Nagendra Chandra Paul was examined as PW 2 who while proving the bainapatra Ext. 1 stated that he wrote the bainapatra. He also stated that he is a deed writer by profession but this Ext. 1 was not written as a professional man. He admitted that he has no licence. He does not know the name of the wife of Madhab Chandra Paul. He also does not know the names of the wives of the Pauls. This PW 2 clearly stated in his evidence that Marani Paul was not the wife of Chandra Kumar Paul. He further stated that bainapatra was written at the instruction of the daughter-in-law and wife of Chandra Kumar Paul. We find that there is a vital contradiction in the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 as regards the scribe of the bainapatra Ext. 1. PW 1 stated that the bainapatra was written by one Jogendra Chandra Paul while PW 2 Nagendra Kumar Paul claimed that he had written the bainapatra. This vital contradiction in the evidence of PW 1 and 2 clearly indicates that the bainapatra Ext. 1 is not genuine. We shall find support in this view from the evidence of PW 3 Abdul Latif Talukder who stated that he signed the bainapatra as attesting witness. PW 4 Rustom Ali Kabiraj also stated that he signed the bainapatra as attesting witness. This was not the case of the plaintiff either in the plaint or in his evidence. PW 4 also stated that the bainapatra was written as instructed by Nitta Nanda Paul. He also stated that the plaintiff purchased the stamp. It appears from the bainapatra Ext. 1 that it was written on a plain paper and not on any stamp though PW 4 stated stamp was purchased by the plaintiff for writing of the bainapatra. From all these evidence, we are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra Ext. 1. We shall now consider the plaintiffs case of possession as asserted in the plaint. To prove his case of possession the plaintiff as PW 1 has not uttered a single word that he was ever in possession of the suit property. It is strange that when the plaintiff based his title on adverse possession, he did not claim possession in his evidence. We have gone between the lines of his evidence and we find that the plaintiff has not uttered a single word as regards his possession in the suit land, far less on the basis of the bainapatra Ext. 1. Since the plaintiff has not stated anything in his evidence as regards his possession of the suit property, there was no occasion of his witnesses to corroborate him on this vital issue. As a matter of fact PW 2 Nagendra Chandra Paul also did not utter a single word about plaintiff’s possession in the suit land. On the other hand, PW 3 and PW 4 clearly deposed in their cross- examination that defendant No. 3 possesses the lands of Pauls by purchase. Since the plaintiff filed the suit claiming acquisition of title by adverse possession, the onus in entirely on him to show by clear and definite evidence that his possession is continuous, open, undisturbed uninterrupted and hostile to the real owner. Here in the present case the plaintiff has not uttered a single word as regards his possession in his evidence. We therefore, find that the plaintiff has failed to prove his possession in the suit land. 

 14. On the otherhand, the contesting defendant No. 3 asserted that the suit land belonged to Chandra Kumar Paul and he purchased the same from him by a bainapatra but as Chandra Kumar Paul died before the execution of a sale deed, the defendant No. 3 continued in possession and subsequently filed a suit against the heirs of Chandra Kumar Paul and obtained a decree from the appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 .which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983. The said judgment has been marked as Ext. 6 in the suit. It appears from Ext. 5 that in Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 filed by the contesting defendant No.3 against Gopal Chandra Paul son of Chandra Kumar Paul, the present plaintiff filed an application for impleading him as a party in the said Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 which was rejected. The contesting defendant No. 3 proves his possession in the suit land in evidence and he was supported by PW 3 and PW4. 

 15. The plaintiff has claimed his title in the suit land by .adverse possession on the basis of the bainapatra Ext. 1 from Marani Paul. We have held that Marani Paul did not acquire any title from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul on the basis of the alleged oral gift and, as such, she has no transferable right to execute the bainapatra Ext. 1. We have also found that the plaintiff has failed to prove the genuineness of the bainaparta Ext. 1 and his possession in the suit land on the basis thereof. Since the plaintiff has no possession in the suit land, the suit for declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession cannot succeed. The learned Subordinate Judge, it appears to us, has not committed any error or illegality in dismissing the plaintiffs suit. 

 16. The learned Subordinate Judge, of course, did not consider the prayer made by the plaintiff as regards declaration that the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 is collusive, void and not binding on the plaintiff. Since we have found that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit land, the plaintiff cannot challenge the decree obtained by defendant No. 3. Further, it appears that this plaintiff unsuccessfully tried to be impleaded in the said suit which was decreed in appellate stage. 

 17. We have found that the plaintiff could not prove his case of acquisition of title by adverse possession and, as such, the plaintiff has no locus-standi to challenge the decree obtained by defendant No.3. Court fees paid are correct.

lawyer:
SS Halder with SS Sarker, Advocates — For the Petitioners.

parties:
Chan Mahmood (Md) & others  ------ Petitioners
Vs
Md Hossain Ali being dead his heirs (Ka) Md Sekander Ali & ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued at the instance of the defendant against the impugned judgment and decree dated 16-2-95 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Tangail in OC Appeal No. 216 of 1990 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-6-1990 passed by the Assistant Judge, Madhupur in Other Suit 37 of 1987 for declaration of title decreeing the suit. 

 2. The suit of the plaintiff, in short, is that, Gowhar Sheikh was the original Raiyot having his 16 annas ownership over 12.42 acres land including the suit land comprising an area of 8.47 acres. The CS Khatian was correctly prepared in the name of said Gowhar Sk Plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Gowhar Sk According to them, the suit land devolved on them and they are in possession. The suit land is part of the land of CS Khatian 31(Ext). The CS Khatian has also been proved and exhibited by the defendants as Ext. C and by the plaintiff as Ext.1 

 3. Plaintiffs'' specific case is that, the land of CS Khatian 31 was divided into three ROR Khatians, that is SA Khatians being 28, 29 and 30. ROR Khatians 28 and 29 were wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. Despite the same, the plaintiffs were in possession of the entire suit land of the said three ROR Khatians. Because of the preparation of said two Khatians 28 and 29 in respect of post of the suit land in favour of the defendants the title of the plaintiffs has been clouded. Therefore, they have filed the suit for declaration of their title alleging that in the month of Agrahayan, 1393 BS when they went to the local Tahsil office to pay rent they found that the said ROR Khatians have been wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. 

 4. Defendants 1-4 contested. Defendants admitted the original rayoti right of Gowhar Sk in the suit land under the CS Khatian. Defendants also admitted the plaintiffs as successive heirs of said Gowhar Sk. Their specific case is that the suit land was auctioned sold in 1930 AD in Rent Realisation case No. 1051C of 1930. The original Zaminder of the suit Khatian Abdul Hamid Chowdhury of the Nagbari Estate, purchased the suit land in auction vide Ext. B, the sale certificate. He possessed and held the land for stipulated period for more than two years and thereafter the defendants took pattan of the suit land from said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. Accordingly, the defendants, as alleged, have acquired their ownership in the suit land and are in possession on payment of land revenue althrough both to the Zamindar and to the Government. 

 7. Plaintiffs' exhibits are 1-1(a), 1(b), 1 (c), 2 part, 2(a)2 and 2(a), Defendants exhibits are A series, which are rent receipts showing payment of rent by them to the Zaminder and to the Government after state acquisition. Ext B is the Bainama (Sale Certificate) and Ext. C is the CS Khatian and C(2) is the ROR Khatian. These are the material exhibits from the side of both parties. Defendants could not file the pattannama or any documentary evidence as to their taking pattan from Abdul Hamid Chowdhury So also defendants failed to produce or file in the court the letter of delivery of possession to complete the alleged auction purchase of the suit auction by Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. The defendants also could not produce any paper or document to show that the suit land originally belonged to Nagbari Estate of Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. 

 9. In this case, the plaintiffs' onus was to prove that they are the heirs of Gowhar Sk and they are in possession. The plaintiffs are admittedly successive heirs of Gowhar Sk. Defendants' onus was to prove the genuineness of the said auction sale of the suit property and that Abdul Hamid Chowdhury was the original Zaminder having rent receiving interest in the suit holding. 

 11. So the defendants, according to the provision of sections 102, 103 and 104 of the Evidence Act, are to prove the original ownership of Abdul Hamid Chowdhury and that he was the decree holder in the rent suit and he made the purchase in the auction sale legally and he settled the suit land to the defendants. 

 12. Mr Halder, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff petitioners, reads the contents of Ext 1 vis-a-vis Ext.0 which is the CS Khatian to me which shows that the property originally did not belong to Abdul Hamid Chowdhury, rather, it belonged to one Shayam Chand Singh and under him Gowhar Sk was in possession as Raiyot. So, the specific case of the defendants as stated above is belied by the contents of Ext. 1 of the plaintiffs which is at the same time Ext. C of the defendants. Thus the plaintiffs succeeded in proving their moot case as to title and the defendants'' case cuts at the root of it. 

 13. The trial Court dismissed the suit finding, inter alia, that the auction sale was valid and the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession. Trial Court held that the defendants could prove that the suit land along with other lands of the said Khatian belonged to Nagbari estate and the suit land was auction sold and was legally purchased by said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury as the Original landlord and later on settled the same to the defendants. This finding of the trial Court is totally beyond the admitted basic title deed namely, the CS Khatian. Therefore, these findings of the trial Court are the result of misreading of evidence, it has been rightly rebutted by the appellate Court. 

 14. Appellate Court has decided the dispute in a very slipshod manner. Appellate Court believed the possession of the plaintiffs and disbelieved the possession of the defendants as the last and final court of fact, considering the evidence both oral and documentary. Appellate Court rightly found that the defendants could not produce any paper as to the rent suit or execution case thereof and also admittedly the defendants could not file letter of delivery of possession. Although SA Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendants, but the same cannot extinguish the title of the plaintiffs who are admittedly the heirs of the original owner said Gowhar Sk. Appellate Court also found that the defendants could not prove their pattan which is the anchor sheet of their case of title from said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. 

 15. Trial Court wrongly found that the suit in the present form for simple declaration was not maintainable. Because the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession, when the plaintiff could prove their possession as found by the appellate Court, the suit for declaration of title is very much maintainable. 

 16. Mr Ramzan Ali Khan, the learned Counsel for the defendant opposite parties, submits that the rent receipt of the defendants although are many in number, but the same were manufactured by forgery by the defendants to grab the suit land although they have no title or possession in the same. Defendants could not show payment of rent of the period from the years 1934-1943, 1945-46, 1950-52 and for the years 1976-87 which also destroys the case of the defendants that they paid rent for all the years from 1930, the alleged years of taking pattan of the suit land by them. Preparation of SA or ROR Khatian and payment of the rent does not create any title in favour of the defendants when the plaintiffs could prove their possession as well, in the suit land. 

 18. Mr Halder, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that although there is no letter of delivery of possession after auction sale of the suit land, the sale certificate being a deed of title as held in 5 DLR 285 in the case of Kalipada Saha and others vs. Nitya Nanda Saha and others even without a letter of delivery of possession the title of the purchaser is complete and, as such, the appellate Court should have found that the defendants acquired good title. In the said decision it has been held by an eminent Judge of this sub-continent Mr Justice Ibrahim as follows : 

 "It is not a deed of title in the sense that it shows the creation of a new right". 

 19. So, in view of the facts and circumstances as stated above, only the boinama Ext. B is not sufficient to decree the title in favour of the defendants. Genuineness of the rent receipts of the defendants are not beyond doubt and because of gap in payment of alleged rent by the defendants they also cannot stand on the footing claiming their title on the basis of adverse possession and no ground has been taken in this revision for adverse possession of the defendants. So, attempt of Mr Halder in this regard ended in futility. It is settled principle of law that when original claim of title is referable to certain documents adverse possession cannot be there (See 10 DLR (SC) 174). It has been found as follows : 

 "Possession is not adverse where original occupation is referable to lawful title". 

 SA Khatian can create presumption of possession but not of title which the CS Khatian can. Both parties adduced oral evidence to prove possession. The appellate Court on appreciation of the same as the last and final court of fact has found the same in favour of the plaintiffs. 

 "Rent receipts their evidentiary value though not documents of title, they are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title". 

 The possession itself can be used for collateral purpose in deciding title. So, possession follows title. Here in this case both title and possession have been found by the appellate Court in favour of the plaintiffs. This case is distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the said case. So that decision is not applicable in this instant case. 

 21. For the reasons and discussions made above, I find that the appellate Court although has passed his judgment in a very slipshod manner, but impliedly has rebutted the findings and decisions of the trial Court both as to the title and possession of the defendants with cogent and well founded legal reasons. Therefore, the appellate Court's judgment does not suffer from any illegality either in fact or in law resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

parties:
Hajee Abdus Sattar ----- Appellant.
vs
Mahiuddin and other ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J : In this appeal by special leave the question for determination is whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division rightly interfered with the appellate Court's Judgment holding that the respondent are tenants of the plaintiff-appellant and that they are stopped from questioning the appellant's title in the suit-premises. The order impugned of the High Court Division is dated 18 January 1984 in Civil Revision No. 184 of 1983 arising out of Title Appeal No. 87 of 1977 of the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali. 

 3. Defendant No.1, (respondent No.1) son of Kala Miah contested the suit denying the appellant's title altogether and setting up a rival claim of title himself on the basis of purchase from one Mohammadullah. He contended that the original owner, Gagan Ali, did not sell the premises to the appellant under any kabala, like Exhibitl, but Gagan Ali made oral transfer of his interest including possession of the suit-land to Mohammadullah and that it is Mohammadullah who, by an unregistered agreement dated 2-6-64 (Exhibit Ka) sold the premises to him on receipt of consideration of Taka 600 and since then he has been possessing it as of his own right. He denied that his father Kala Miah was a tenant under the appellant or that he got the premises by inheritance from his father and, as such, no question of his holding over as a tenant of the appellant arose. 

 4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence both oral and documentary held that Kala Mia was not a tenant under the plaintiff, that defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit property on the basis of his purchase from Mohammadullah who, on his turn, had purchased it from Gagan Ali and that there was no landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants and on these findings he dismissed the suit by judgment dated 8-5-74. The plaintiff preferred an appeal but the appeal was dismissed by the sub-ordinate Judge against whose decision the plaintiff filed a revisional application being Revision Case No. 387 of 1981 before the High Court Division and the latter, on allowing the application, remanded the appeal to the Subordinate Judge for rehearing. Thus after re-haring the appeal the learned Sub-ordinate Judge by his Judgment dated 2-4-83 allowed the appeal, reversed the trial Court's judgment and decreed the suit finding, among other things, that the plaintiff got title from Gagan Ali by the Sale deed Exhibit 1, that the plaintiff inducted Kala Mia, father of defendant No. 1, as tenant by the registered Agreement, Exhibit 3, that on the death of Kala Mia his heirs including defendant No. 1 held over possession as tenants but defaulted in the payment of rent. This decision of the appellate Court was again challenged by defendant No.1, in revision namely Civil Revision No. 184 of 11983 and the learned Single Judge, by the impugned judgment, reversed the appellate Court's decision and restored that of the trial Court. 

 5. Mr Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the appellant, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge, particularly his interference in revision with the finding of facts arrived at by the lower Appellate Court on the question whether the respondents were tenants by holding-over' under the appellant. The learned Advocate has criticised the learned Single Judge for, what he terms, illegally rejecting the appellant's documentary evidence including a clear admission of the respondent that he was a tenant under the appellant and also for the view taken by the learned Single Judge that in the absence of satisfactory proof of payment of rent the respondent was not a tenant of the appellant whose registered instruments including the registered Lease Agreement have been arbitrarily rejected. The learned Advocate contends that in view of creation of the tenancy in favour of Kala Mia, father of the respondent, the latter was estoppel from questioning the appellant's title under section 116 of the Evidence Act. 

 116. No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall, during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property; and no person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time when such license was given." 

 The estoppels as described in this section are known as tenant's estoppels or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person the neither he nor anybody claiming through his shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it. This principle of law has been nicely expounded by Jessel MP in Re Siringer's Estate, page 384 LR 6 Ch 9 in the following works: 

 "Where a man having no title obtains possession of land under demise by a man in possession who assumes to give him a title as tenant, he cannot deny his deny his landlord's title. This is a perfectly intelligible doctrine. He took possession under a contract to pay rent so long as he held possession under the landlord, and to give it up at the end of the term to the landlord, and having taken it in that way he is not allowed to say that the man whose title he admits and under whose title he took possession has not a title. That is a well-established doctrine. That is estoppels by contract." 

 Sometimes it is found that after entering into possession as a tenant a person, from some motive, defaults in the payment of rent and when the question of eviction is raised he takes the plea that he is not a tenant for there is no evidence that he ever paid rent to the landlord. Such a device cannot carry him anywhere in view of the basic principle that once he is found to have entered into possession as tenant non-payment of rent shall not be interpreted as non-existence of the tenancy. Payment of rent is one among many other proofs of a tenancy. Mere non-payment of rent does not terminate the tenancy or make the possession of the tenant adverse to the landlord, as has been rightly held in the case of JM Singh vs Baldeo Singh, 49 IA 299. This position is based on the footing that once relation of landlord and tenant is established it is presumed to continue, and the burden of proving that it has ceased is on the person who alleges it to have ceased. Section 116 in express language precludes the tenant from questioning his landlord's title during the continuance of the tenancy: this section however does not debar him from doing so after it is shown by him that the landlord's title has been lost or extinguished since then. But if he himself claims title he must first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken the lease. Again, if the landlord determines the tenancy on any ground but the tenant continues to stay on still the tenant will be stopped from questioning the landlord's title unless he restores possession to the landlord who had put him into possession. 

 8. Registered Agreement Exhibit 3 is the evidence of creation of a tenancy by the appellant in favour of Kala Mia at a monthly rent of Taka 45. The learned Single Judge has observed that through this exhibit is a registered Agreement. It does not by itself prove the tenancy. What appears to be meant by this observation is that the Agreement even if genuine might not have been acted upon. The respondent questioned the execution of the Agreement and also alleged that it was not acted upon. So far as the execution is concerned, besides PW 1 (the appellant), PW 5 a Deed- writer has deposed that he had written this Agreement, which was executed in his presence. As to whether it was acted upon, besides the evidence of PW 1, there is the evidence of a number of witnesses including PWs 2, 3 and 4 PW2 is Kala Mia's son-in-law, that is, he is brother-in-law of the respondent (defendant No-1); he has supported the appellant's case that Kala Mia was a tenant under the appellant and resided in the house carrying on cloth- business there. Evidence of PW 2 was sought to be discarded on the ground that he married a stepsister of defendant No.1 and as such he is hostile to him. But there is no evidence whatever that there was any clash of interest or enmity between defendant No.1 and PW 2; and if there were any strained relationship between them, it appears, it is due to the fact that PW 2, through a relation, came to the Court to depose against his disclosing the truth and not supporting his claim of rival title by the unregistered Agreement (Exhibit Ka) which has been challenged by the appellant to be antedated PW 3 is an independent witness. He is a practicing lawyer having residence near the suit premises. He claims to know both the parties. He has stated that the premises belonged to the appellant who possessed it through different tenants and that he saw Kala Mia possessing it as a tenant of the appellant PW 4, Hashmatullah, says that the possessed the premises as tenant of the appellant before the structure was destroyed by fire, that is, prior to Kala Mia's tenancy. On consideration of evidence the lower Appellate Court held that the Agreement, Exhibit 3, was not only genuine but it was acted upon. Case of the respondent (Kala Mia's son) is that his father did not take the tenancy, but he himself purchased the premises from one Mohammadullah who is DW 2 Mohammadullah's evidence is that he sold it to the respondent by the unregistered Agreement, Exhibit (Ka" as already stated on 2-6-64, that is, about three months earlier than Kala Mia's registered Agreement, Exhibit. If Exhibit 'Ka' is relied upon, the we find two tenants simultaneously for the same premises, one is the father and the other is the son Case of the appellant is that Exhibit Ka is a fraudulent and antedated document. Even if it were not fraudulent and antedated, still the broad fact remains that under this Agreement no interest passed to Kala Mia's son unless it is shown that Mohammadullah had any right, title or interest in the premises himself. Mohammadullah claims title from Gagan Ali Bepari, but there is no paper to show that Gagan Ali Bepari had transferred the premises to Mohammadullah. Secondly, Gagan Ali Bepari could not have made such transfer in 1964 as he had already transferred his entire interest in the premises to the appellant by an earlier registered Sale-deed 8-12-53, Exhibit 1. The claim of the respondent that he purchased it from Mohammadullah is negative by Exhibit 1 read with the supporting oral evidence. Evidence of Mohammadullah has been challenged on another ground; his elder brother PW 4 Hashmatullah has deposed that he had taken lease of the premises from the appellant as a month to month tenant by a registered Agreement dated 13-6-55 (Exhibit 3A) and continued their till the structure was gut- ted by fire in 1964. He has further deposed that Mohammadullah, his younger brother, was at that time a mere student. Thus it appears that Mohammadullah, respondent's vendor, was not even a tenant in the premises but his elder brother was the tenant. To avoid that question of validity of the alleged transfer of the property by Mohammadullah to him, the respondent went to the extent of denying the genuineness of appellant's title under, Exhibit 1, the registered sale-deed and it has been argued that this Sale-deed was either fraudulent or it was not acted upon. To counter this contention evidence, both oral and documentary, has been led by the appellant. It is that after the purchase under Exhibit 1, and when Hashmatullah was a tenant, the premises was sold in auction for recovery of some public dues and it is the appellant who got the sale set aside. In this connection the appellant filed an order of the Board of Revenue setting aside the sale at his instance. That order is Exhibit 5 dated 30 January. 160. PW 3, the lawyer, has supported the appellant's case saying that he was engaged by the appellant in the proceedings for setting aside the auction sale under Exhibit 5 the learned Single Judge has observed that this document got no direct bearing on the issue in question. If the tenancy of Kala Mia is in question, this document is not so much relevant, but if the appellant-land-lord's title is challenged, this document is very much relevant. We therefore find that the respondent with a view to boosting up his story of purchase from Mohammadullah, who was nobody to make any such transfer, raised out of motive the dispute about the appellant's original title under Exhibit 1, by the registered sale-deed, executed by Gagan Ali Bepari. Curiously enough, it is Gagan Ali Bepari from whom Mohammadullah claims title by oral purchase at a subsequent- date. In the circumstances, the appellate Court's finding that both Exhibits 1 and 3 are genuine documents and were acted upon is a finding based on proper consideration of evidence and as such this finding was not open for re-opening in the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. 

 9. Mr Asrarul Hossain has laid considerable stress on Exhibits 4 and 4(a) which purportedly contain an admission of the respondent (defendant No.1) that he was a tenant under the appellant. These exhibits are certified copies of two applications of the respondent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) praying for settlement to the suit-premises from the Government, the ultimate owner. Both the appellant and the respondent (defendant No.1) prayed for settlement from the Government in 1973 where upon two separate cases were started which ended ultimately in favour of the appellant, obviously in view of the appellant's possessory right from Gagan Ali Bepari for a long time. The question raised here, however, is not as to who got the settlement from the Government, in both these applications, Exhibits. 4 and 4(a), filed about six years after his father Kala Mia's death, the respondent (defendant No.1) stated that he was a tenant of the appellant, Haji Abdus Sattar, who by misrepresentation had created the tenancy though he had no title, that because of this defect of title, he was offering himself as a candidate for settlement in view of the fact that he had been running a cloth-shop in the premises for a long time. This is a clear admission and it estoppel him from denying the appellant's title in the premises. To wriggle out of this tight comer, he has contended that the documents exhibits 4 & 4(a) are not correct copies of his applications to the Revenue Authorities. The learned Single Judge has observed that these copies of the applications were not legally proved, that they are private documents and further that attention of the respondent was not drawn to the statement contained in these supplications, and as such the question of binding him with the statement therein does not arise. This observation, we find, got no legal or factual basis. For these are certified copies of applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for settlement, who after necessary endorsement, incorporated them into the record of the Settlement Case and issued certified copies thereof in accordance with law the originals of the applications cannot be produced or obtained by anybody unless a Court calls for them. These certified copies were filed as exhibits in this suit in presence of respondent who them raised objection, but the Court ignoring his objection marked them as exhibits 4 and 4(a). Again, while deposing in Court as DW 1 he himself drew his attention to these documents stating in his examination-in-chief that these were not true copies his applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner. In the circumstances, there was no necessity for drawing his further attention to them during cross-examination. As to the authenticity of these certified copies, the respondent did not apply to the Court to lodge in complaint under section 195 CrPC against the appellant on a charge of forgery who produced or filed in evidence these documents in a judicial proceeding Such a complaint may be filed under section 195 (1) (c) CrPC even now if the respondent dares to move the Court for that purpose. These documents issued and certified to be true copies by an authorised officer of the Government are admissible in evidence. The statement contained therein as described above is an admission within the meaning of section 20 of the Evidence Act and the respondent is bound by his admission that he was a tenant of the appellant who allegedly got no valid title to the premises. 

 10. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate for the respondent, has tried to make out a case of total non-payment of rent and has contended that in the absence of reliable evidence that rent was ever paid to the appellant it cannot he said that any tenancy was created or the Agreement Exhibit 3, purportedly creating the tenancy was acted upon. Evidence in this connection is that Kala Mia paid rent so long be was alive and after his death his heirs, the defendants, became irregular in payment of rent and ultimately stopped it. PW 2 has stated that Kala Mia during his life-time had engaged him to AD-14 look after his cloth-shop and to pay rent for the premises and that the respondent paid rent for 14 months at a time by Exhibit 6. He has also deposed that he had been authorised in writing by his father in-law to act as his Assistant in the cloth-business (Exhibit 13). These two documents have been seriously challenged as fabrication for the purpose of the suit, PW 2 has, of course, denied the suggestion as to fabrication of Exhibits. 6 and 13; but the payment of rent for 14 months at a time and non-production of any receipts for payment of rent for the earlier period create suspicion in the genuineness of the receipt Exhibit 6. But I have already observed at the beginning that mere non-payment of rent does not snap landlord and tenant relationship and that non-payment of rent will not enable a tenant to question landlord's title unless he discontinues the tenancy and restores possession to the landlord. If mere non-payment of rent is taken as proof of non-existence of landlord and tenant relationship grave consequences will follow, for an unscrupulous tenant upon entering a premise as a tenant will deliberately as a convenient time. Mr TH Khan has contended that there is no evidence of the respondents holding over and that if the evidence as to payment of rent by Exhibit 6 is rejected no tenancy under the appellant exists. Answer to this contention is contained in the principle enunciated already in paragraph 6 above. It is that once a tenancy is created, it will be presumed that it is continuing, unless it is shown that it has ceased. The tenancy was created in favour of Kala Mia on whose death his heirs (including defendant No.1) continued to possess the premises. This is "holding over." For without Kala Mia's tenancy they could not have entered upon possession particularly when the claim of independent title by purchase has fallen through. They say that they did not pay any rent to the appellant but such non- payment of rent hardly improves their case, for the tenancy continues even if payment of rent is not made. 

 "A tenancy-at-will is determinable at the will of either landlord or tenant and is a personal relation between the original landlord or tenant and is determined by the death of either of them." 

 It is obvious that such a tenancy is not heritable in the sense that on the death of a tenant his heirs are not under any legal obligation to pay rent to the landlord or to continue the tenancy, in the same way, as the landlord is not bound to keep the lease alive. Both the parties are at liberty to discontinue the tenancy. If the heirs of late tenant continue to stay on, but do not pay rent they shall not be permitted to say that the landlord has no title and in case they themselves claim title they must first of all restore possession to the land-lord an act which has not been done in this case. As such they have been rightly held to be tenants by holding over.
justice_names: Mr. Justice F. K. M. Abdul Munim

parties:
Abdul Gafur
Vs.
Ali Akbar & Another
full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J: — This Rule his arisen out of a judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali, reversing those of the learned Munsif, Noakhali, passed in a suit for declaration that the defendant No. 1 was the benamder of the plaintiff in respect of the kabala dated 10.1.1957 and that the kabala executed by the defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant No. 2 did not create any title, and it was not binding against the plaintiff. 

 7. The learned Advocate has lastly submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in not considering that the defendant No. 1 though found to be an ostensible owner of the kabala land, the defendant No. 2 being a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration and having taken reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had the power to make the transfer and that the purchaser had purchased the land in good faith, the kabala of the defendant No. 2 could not be set aside under the provisions of section 41 of the Transfer of property Act. According to the learned Advocate the original Title deed dated 16.1.57 having stood in the name of defendant No. 1 and the M.R.R. having been prepared and finally published without any objection from the plaintiff in the name of the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff having allowed these to continue in defendant No. l's name, the defendant No. 2 having purchased the suit land from the defendant No. 1 in good faith for consideration, the defendant No. 2's right, title and possession was well protected. 

 8. This point though not raised by any of the parties in the courts below either in the trial court or in the appellate court, yet I permitted the learned advocate to argue the point. Certain facts stare on the face of the record. The land under the impugned kabala was purchased when the defendant No. I was a small boy of 7/8 years. The possession of the land has been found against the defendant. The impugned kabala has come from the custody of the plaintiff. The defendant No. 2 could not show that the rents of the disputed land have ever been paid by the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 2 has alleged that M.R.R. being in the name of the defendant No. 1, the transfer of the land by the impugned kablala of the defendant No. 2 ought to have been held to be in good faith. He has also submitted that since the land has been allowed to remain in the name of ostensible owner, the purchase should be presumed to be in good faith. Even if presumption is attached to such purchase facts of the case clearly indicate that the transfer in favour of the defendant No. 2 was not in good faith. Moreover in the written statement though the defendant has made out a case of a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration, no positive evidence as to his bonafide has been proved. It is in evidence that the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 resided in the same house and that plaintiff and defendant No. 2 are first contusions and it is therefore likely in all probability that the defendant No. 2 knew that the plaintiff purchased the land in the benami of his minor son. Further, the defendant No. 2 purchased the land without the title deed of his vendor and without ascertaining who paid the rents in order to indicate good faith.

parties:
Gopal Chandra Mondol ----- Appellant
Vs.
Lashmat Dasi ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
The plaintiff's case may briefly be stated as follows: That the suit property originally belonged to Gour Majhi who had 2 sons namely Defendant No. 1 and Nagar Mondal. Nagar Mondal pre-deceased his father leaving the plaintiff Debendra Mondal as his only son. After the death of Gour Majhi the plaintiff as grand-son of Gour Majhi and defendant No. 2 Jagadish as his son became the heirs of Gour Majhi in equal shares. The plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 have been possessing the suit land jointly as co-sharers but due to some difficulties the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 1 for an amicable partition of the land in suit but the defendant did not agree and hence this suit for partition. Jagadish defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement Defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5, the transferees from Lakhan Dasi, daughter of defendant No. 1 also appeared and contested the suit by filing another joint written statement. Defendant No. 1 in his written statement denied all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia that the plaintiff is a stranger to the property, having no right, title, interest and possession of the land in suit. It was further alleged that the suit land originally belonged to Gour Majhi who died leaving only one son defendant No. 1 and he had no other son by the name of Nagar Mondal. The said Nagar Mondal was the son of Gour Majhi's brother Keroly Majhi, Nagar Mondal, son of Keroly Majhi married the daughter of one Hari Charan Mondal and lived in Hari Charan Mondal's house as a domesticated son-in-law. Nagar Mondal always lived in his father-in-law's house leaving behind the plaintiff as his son and the plaintiff also had always been living in that house of his maternal uncle and not in the suit homestead. The plaintiff has no interest in the suit and being not a co-sharer the suit needs to be dismissed. Defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5 contended that Gour  Majhi died leaving only one son namely Jagadish (Defendant No. 1) who died leaving one daughter in Lakhan Desi and that Jagadish during his Iife time made a gift of the suit land in favour of Lakhan Dasi by a registered deed of gift and Lakhan Dasi sold the suit land to defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5 by a registered sale deed and they have been possessing the land in suit since the said purchase. Their further case was that Nagar Mondal was the son of Gour Majhi's brother Keroly Majhi and never the son of Gour Majhi, that the plaintiff was the grand-son of Keroly. Majhi, brother of Gour Majhi and not of Gour Majhi and hence the plaintiff has no right, title and interest as a co-sharer in the property of Gour Majhi. 

 2. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary came to the view that the defendant No. 1 had the onus to prove that the plaintiff was not the grand-son of Gour Majhi and he having failed to prove so the plaintiff would be considered to have proved that he was the son of Gour Majhi and that being the position the plaintiff would be a co-sharer of the suit land and therefore would be entitled to partition, holding further that the absence of the name of the plaintiff in the rent receipts, S A. Khatian and land acquisition case records, would not prove that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer and would not deprive the plaintiff from his share in the suit land. In that view of the matter the suit was decreed on contest without costs, in preliminary form.
