In the judgment, the Adalat however, found, in so many words, that the property was mortgaged.

lawyer:
For the petitioner: Mr. A.K.M. Asaduzzaman
For the opposite parties : Mr. S. Goswami with Mr. Md. Sohorab Hossain
parties:
Sadek Uddin Chowdhury and another  ------  Petitioner.
Versus 
Md. Anowarul Hoque Chowdhury and another  ------  Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Shamsul Huda, J. : This Rule is directed on an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendant appellant petitioners against the judgment and decree dated 30.4.1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 222 of 1993, affirming the judgment and decree dated 21.8.1993 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Naogaon in Other Class Suit No. 125 of 1.991 decreeing the suit. 

 2. The facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule in brief are that, the opposite parties being plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 125 of 1991 in the court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Naogaon for declaration of title in the suit land, contending inter alia that the suit land originally belonged to Niroda Sundari and Dasya in equal share  Mrinalini Dasya orally relinquished her share in favour of Niroda Sundari who became the owner of 16 annas share in the suit land. On 23.6.1947 Niroda Sundari sold the same to one Haider Ali by a registered sale deed No. 3142. Thereafter Haider Ali sold the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1-2 through registered sale deed dated 29.8.1968 and handed over possession to them. to ignorance of Haider Ali thy land was wrongly recorded in the name of Niroda Sundari in S. A. Khatian. Since the Patnitola Sub-registrar's Office was burnt during war of liberation they could not obtain original copy of the sale deed and as such they have filed the certified copy of the aforesaid deed, which was obtained before war of liberation. During R. S. operation it was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendants along with the names of the plaintiffs and quantum of land in R.S. Plot No. 221 was recorded as 1.17 acres in place of 1.77 acres of land. The R.S. record was wrong. 

 3. The defendant petitioners herein contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alia, that admittedly Niroda Sundari was the original owner of the suit land and the plain-tiffs' father and the father of the defendants were full brothers who purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs and the defendants as well, in equal share and in R.S. Khatian the land was correctly recorded in their names. 

 4. The trial court decreed the suit. The defendant petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 222 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Naogaon challenging the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Naogaon which was heard, on transfer, by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Naogaon, who by the impugned judgment dated 30.4.1997 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial court. The petitioners preferred the instant Civil Revision against the impugned judgment and obtained the Rule. 

 5. Mr. A.K.M. Asaduzzaman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the courts below without dis-cussing any evidence whatsoever decreed the suit. The trial court did not discuss any evidence and arrived at an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice, inasmuch as the learned Assistant Judge failed to consider that the plaintiffs did not produce the original deed of their title, claimed to have been executed and registered in favour of them by Haider Ali. On the other hand the defendants claimed that the suit land originally belonged to Niroda Sundari from whom their father and the plaintiffs father jointly purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs and themselves in equal share and there was no existence of any deed of transfer being executed and registered by Haider Ali. As the father of the plaintiff was the elder brother of the father of the defendants and he being clever person and Chairman of the local Union Parishad for more than 30 years, all the documents of their properties were kept in his custody. The plaintiffs in collusion with their father has suppressed the original deed and since the Patnitola Sub-registrar's Office was burnt during war of liberation they have created certified copy of the sale deed showing Haider Ali as the vendor of the sale deed but in fact there was no such deed. All the deeds filed by the plaintiffs in the trial court are forged and created for the purpose of the suit. He further submits that in R.S. record the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and the defendants in equal share on the basis of title deeds and physical possession and they have shown the suit land in their respective statement filed to the Government in respect of ownership of the land. He further submits that the trial court did not all consider the evidence of the defendants. By oral evidence also the defendants were able to prove their right, title and possession in the suit land. The Appellate Court below has also committed the same mistake in not discussing any evidence and recording independent findings which is a violation of mandatory pro-vision of law i.e. Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus the judgments of both the courts below suffer from legal infirmities, such as misreading and non reading of evidence. The learned Advocate submits that in this circumstances the suit may be sent back on remand to the Appellate Court below for writing a proper judgment. In this regard he refers to the case reported in AIR. 1969 (Rajastan) 9. On careful reading of the aforesaid decision it appears that the same has no manner of application in the present case inasmuch as the said suit was sent back on remand as the court below wrongly excluded the statement of the plaintiff from evidence. 

 10. It appears from the plaint that the plaintiffs claimed their title by purchase of the suit land from one Haider Ali, who purchased the same from Niroda Sundari and they have claimed that the R.S. record was wrong and in R.S. Plot No. 221 of Khatian No. 35, the quantum of land was recorded as 1.17 acres in place of 1.77 acres of land. It appears from the written statement filed by the Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that they claimed their title through purchase from Niroda Sundari by their father and uncle, the father of the plain-tiffs, jointly. In paragraph No. 6 of their written statement they have stated that their father died in the year 1964-65. In paragraph No. 9 of the written statement they have claimed that the deed of title of the plaintiffs was forged, which the Defendant No. 1 would prove at the time of trial and also prayed for impounding the certified copy of the sale deed, being filed by the plaintiff. In paragraph 14 of the written statement the defendants claimed that while their father and the father of the plaintiffs were in joint Mess they have purchased the suit land in the names of their respective sons from Niroda. Sundari in equal share. 

 11. P.W. 1 Ashraful Hoque Chowdhury proved his title supporting the case as stated in the plaint. In cross-examination he has clearly stated that as the Patnitola Sub-registrar's Office was burnt during the war of liberation. They could not obtain the original copy of the deed of title but they obtained the certified copy of the sale deed earlier which was filed in the court from their custody and the same was marked as Exhibit 1(Ka). On perusal of exhibit 1(Ka) it appears that the certified copy of the sale deed was obtained on 31.1.1968. The sale deed of Niroda Sundari was marked as Exhibit 1, which was registered in the year 1947 and the same was admitted in evidence without formal proof as it was old document of over 30 years. Exhibit 2 is the D.C.R. in respect of Mutation Case No. 308 of 1979-80 in favour of the plaintiffs. Exhibit 3- 3(ka)-3(Cha) are the rent receipts obtained by the plaintiff and their father. Exhibit-3- 3(Ka)L3(Cha) prove that the father of the plaintiffs paid rent to the government some time in the name of Niroda Sundari and thereafter in the name of the plain-tiffs. Exhibit-6 is the certified copy of the notice of land transfer in respect of the sale deed being executed and registered by Haider Ali in favour of the plaintiffs. 

 13. On due consideration of the documentary evidences on record in juxtaposition with the cross-examination of D.W. 1 it has been clearly proved that the claim of the defendants are down right false because the sale deed being executed and registered by Haider All was registered in favour of the plaintiffs on 29.1.1968 but admittedly the father of the defendants died in the year 1965. So the question of joint purchase by the father of the plaintiffs and the father of the defendants does not arise at all and this single fact falsify the claim of the defendants. The plaintiffs proved its case by producing both oral and documentary evidence. Exhibit 1 being supported by exhibit 6 being an age old document of over 30 years. It has presumptive value under Section 90 of the Evidence Act and the Exhibit 1(Ka), the certified copy of the original sale deed being admitted in evidence without objection in the trial court and as such no objection can be raised at this stage challenging the legality and propriety of the said certified copy of the sale deed. At the same time in the written statement the defendants have taken bur-den of proof that the certified copy of the sale deed, Exhibit I (Ka) as forged and fraudulent but the defendants failed to prove the same and as such the certified copy of an old document of over 30 years old having presumptive value under Section 90 of the Evidence Act and admissible in evidence. Exhibit 1(Ka) cannot be thrown out of consideration and rent receipts being filed by the plaintiffs are the collateral evidence of their possession being followed by title. 

 14. From the discussion made above it can be safely concluded that the plaintiffs were able to prove their title and possession in the suit land both by oral and documentary evidence. On the other hand, the defendants by their own evidence have disproved their case.

parties:
Mrs. Wahida Begum & Ors. ----- Petitioners
Versus
Tajul Islam & Ors. ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
5. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing a joint written statement, Their main case is that the deed of Ekrarnama was neither executed nor presented nor registered by the defendant No. 3. They had no knowledge of existence of the said deed of Ekrarnama. Rather, they purchased the suit land by registered sale deeds dated 05-07-75 and 28-02-79 from the defendant No. 3 with the knowledge and consent of the plaintiff The plaintiff attested their sale deeds. Their further case is that the transaction between the plaintiff and defendant No. 3 is an out and out sale. There is no question of any mortgage ever entered into by the plaintiff and defendant No. 3. The defendants No, 1 and 2 further claimed to be bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama. They asserted that the plaintiff was estopped from raising any question as to any sort of mortgage and thereby not entitled to any decree. 

 12. The case of the plaintiff was that by 3 registered sale deeds exhibits 2, 2 (A) and 2 (B), he transferred the suit land to defendant 3 on 22.04,74 and the defendant 3 in his turn, by another deed of conveyance registered, exhibit 1 on the same date agreed to reconvey the said land to the plaintiff on receipt of Taka 6,000. Defendant 3 or defendants 1 and 2 did not reconvey the suit land even on demands. So, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit on 21.02.82 for recovery of the suit land. as he was entitled to restoration of the land under Section-95 read with Section-95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for the sale by the deeds exhibits 2 to 2 (B) with the agreement to reconvey, Ekrarnama, exhibit 1 must be construed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years. 

 15. The trial court held that the deeds of sale and the agreement for reconveyance together constitutes an usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years under Sections-95 and 95A of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act. and that the defendants 1 and 2 was aware of the Ekrarnama as they admitted that they knew the original title deeds of defendant 3 i.e. exhibits 2, 2A and 2B were in the custody of the plaintiff . 

 24. Now, let me see how far the finding of the appellate court that the defendants 1 and 2 are purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama is based on evidence be record and the law. Are their transactions really protected either under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act or under Section-115 of the Evidence Act? If one wants to be protected under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act, he is required to prove that he took all reasonable care to ascertain the title of his vendor. He inquired at least in the local Sub-Registrar's office to know if the land had any charge or encumbrance or not to establish his bona fide. He would naturally try to get all the documents of title and possession from his vendor. Onus is very heavy on him. There is no onus on the other side, as was wrongly placed by the appellate court. The law is now settled. Section-41 T P Act is an exception to ordinary rule that the transferor cannot convey a greater title to the transferee than he himself has and has to be construed strictly. If any one seeks. protection purportedly either under Section-41 of the Transfer of property Act or tinder of the Evidence Act, he must prove the facts entitling him the benefits under either of the laws. He is required to prove that 'he, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transfer or had power to make the transfer, acted in good faith.' I am supported by the authorities in case of Sunder lcuer v Udey Ram, reported in AIR 1944 Allahabad 42 (page 54 c. d) and Ambabai v. H R Dant reported in AIR 1948 Nagpur 367 (pares 50 and 51). The defendants 1 and 2 pleaded that they were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama. But they did neither plead nor lead any evidence that they took any steps to ascertain the title of their vendor, defendant 3 or their purchased land, i.e. the suit land did not have any charge or encumbrance. They did not make any inquiry even in the local registration office. They did not want to get the documents of title or possession. In their deeds, exhibit A(2) and A(3) though executed and registered about four years apart, it is written in verbatim, to trace the title, the defendant 3 is খরিদ সূত্রে মালিক দখলকার ও মালিক বটে’ This vital fact of purchase from the plaintiff was deliberately suppressed exhibits A(2) and A(3). Purpose was very clear, not to divulge the knowledge about the Ekrarnama. In his deposition, defendant 1 as DW-1 stated that the plaintiff transferred the land to the defendant 3 by an out and out sale. In cross-examination, he admitted that defendant 3 on being asked told him that the original Kabala was lying with the plaintiff. He did not try to obtain the Kabala. Defendant 2 as DW-2 deposed in the same vein that original Kabala was with the plaintiff and he did not try to get the Kabala. Both of them, however, stated that they purchased seeing the copy of the Kabla. But they did not adduce the copy to probe their bona fide it is, therefore, cult to accept such an explanation. 

 The defendants' 1 and 2 did not only take any reasonable care either to ascertain the title of their vendor, defendant 3 or to find if the land had any charge or encumbrance but also suppressed in their deeds from whom their vendor, defendant 3 got the land. In view above evidences, the defendants 1 and 2 cannot be held to be bona fide purchasers without notice and as such, protected under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 27. I have examined the single bench decision in the case of Tazal Hoque v. Md. Allan reported in 17 DLR 613 as cited by Mr. Salek. After the decision, I find, the law on usufructuary mortgage has undergone a change on insertion of Section-95A in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the President Order No. 88 of the 1972. During the appeal, the plaintiff, Sultan Ahmed died on 18.05.91. The present petitioners were substituted in his place. Now, the petitioners who have also the covenant under the Ekrarnama as quoted above to get reconveyance have become entitled to restoration of possession of the entire suit land as prayed for. Moreover, the defendants 1 and 2 have not been found to be bona fide purchasers without notice of the Ekrarnama. Facts of the case are also quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case. So, the trial court rightly held that the sale deeds exhibits 2 series along with the deed of agreement, Ekrarnama, exhibit 1 do in fact constitute an usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years and that the defendants 1 and 2 were aware of the Ekrarnama. The decision of the trial court that the plaintiff is entitled to get restoration of possession of the suit land from the defendants 1 and 2 under Section-95 read with Section-95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is accordingly affirmed.

parties:
Mustafa Kamal Bhuiyan and others ----- Petitioner
Vs
Lutfunnahar Begum and 67 others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22-2-93 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Comilla (in-Charge) in Title Appeal No. 261 of 1990 allowing the said appeal and sending the suit back on remand to the trial Court for fresh decision on setting aside the judgment and decree dated 30-7-90 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Comilla in Partition Suit No. 113 of 1982 dismissing the suit. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing joint written statement. The defendant Nos. 12 and 40 also contested the suit by filing another set of written statement. In both the sets of written statement, the defendants denied all the material allegations made in the plaint and stated that Abdul Gani Bhuiyan had not been the benamder of his son Aftabuddin and he purchased 2.27 acres of land out of his fund and own interest. Claim of the plaintiff of the defendant No. 10's inheriting 1.59-21/55 acres of land from his father and mother is absolutely false. Defendant also described the Hcba-bill-Ewaz deed in favour of the plaintiff as fraudulent transaction and asserted that the plaintiff did not acquire any right, title and possession over the said gifted land. 

 "23. Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the Appellate Court may, if it thinks fit, by order remand the case, and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, with directions to re-admit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit; and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand. 

 (2) Subject as aforesaid, the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein". 

 18. Under section 107 of the Code the appellate Court is vested with the power to determine a case finally and also to remand case. Sub-section 2 of section 107 of the Code lays down that the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein. 

 19. The question now falls for determination is whether the lower appellate Court was justified in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh decision. Record of the suit was called for by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule. The lower appellate Court in remanding the suit to the trial Court observed that though the original title deeds of the benami transaction matter had been filed by the defendant Nos. 9-11, the plaintiff at least was required to file the certified copies of those title deeds. On perusal of the record it appears that the title deeds of the benami transaction had been filed by the defendant No. 10 and those two documents were of the year 1914 and 1917 i.e. 30 years old documents. The said two documents were exhibited as Exhibit Nos. D(1) and D(3). The defendant No. 10 is no other than the son of Aftabuddin and husband of the plaintiff and it is the positive case of the plaintiff that her husband defendant No. 10 gifted the divisible 1.10 acres of land to her by registered Heba-bil-Ewaz deed and it was natural that the custody of those two documents would be with the defendant No. 10. The said two documents were filed in the court from the custody of defendant No. 10. Thus it appears that the lower appellate Court misdirected itself in its approach on the question of non-filing of the certified copies of the deeds of benami transaction and the order remanding the suit to trial Court for a decision on this point suffers from a gross error of law. 

 20. The lower appellate Court found fault with the trial Court in not framing any issue on the question of benami character of the said two deeds. The appellate Court found that the plaintiff did not pray for a declaration of title of the benami character of the kabala deeds. The plaintiff though filed an application for amendment of the plaint in the appellate Court seeking the relief of declaration of title of benami character of the said two deeds the appellate Court did not decide the amendment matter and left the matter for decision by the trial Court. The plaintiff suit being a suit for partition, the question of benami character of the two deeds could be gone into and well decided by the appellate Court and a separate relief of declaration of title on the question of benami character of the deeds was not required and even if there was an application filed by the painful-petitioner for amendment of the plaint incorporating the relief of declaration of title and that application also could be disposed of by the appellate Court and appellate Court was quite competent enough to dispose of the said amendment matter. The order of remand passed by the appellate Court on this score is also unwarranted. 

 33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 22-2-1993 passed in Title Appeal No. 261 of 1990 is hereby set aside and the case is sent back on remand to the lower appellate Court [or disposal of the same touching all points. The appellate Court is also directed to dispose of the appeal preferably within 3(Three) months from the date of the receipt of the record.

parties:
Motasim Ali Chowdhury ------ Appellant
Vs.
Md Ismail  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rouf J: This appeal, following leave, by the plaintiff is from the judgment and order dated 13-1-93 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.826 of 1989 making the Rule absolute and setting aside thereby the order dated 16-8-89 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.226 of 1985 (originally numbered as Title Suit No.326 of 1982 of the Court of the Munsif, First Court, Dhaka) allowing amendment to the plaint. 

 2. The plaintiff, initially, sought for declaration of his title to and recovery of khas possession against the defendant in respect of 0.01-1/4 acres of land, equivalent to 512 square feet, from the extreme western portion of suit plot No. 110 out of his purchased land of 0.08-1/4 acres, purchased on 24-3-64 from Hazi Moran Ali Bepari by a registered kabala, It is alleged, inter alia, that the defendant is an unauthorised and illegal possessor of a portion of plot No.936 adjacent west of suit plot No.110, that in the month of February 1972 the defendant forcibly encroached upon the western part of the suit plot by constructing a semi pucca building thereon and he again on 20-9-81 encroached further area by extending the said semi pucca building. In the plaint the plaintiff described the suit land to be 512 square feet equivalent to 0.01-1/4 acres by annexing a sketch map. 

 8. It is already noted that initially the plaintiff sought for declaration of his title to and recovery of possession of 0.012 acres equivalent to 512 square feet out of his purchased land of 0.08-1/4 acres, which has been shown in his kabala. But he claims on the basis of boundary given in the kabala 0.0932 acres under his possession. By the amendment in question the plaintiff in fact, has sought for incorporating 0.03 acres of land with his aforesaid kabala land of 0.08-1/4 making a case for his purchased land of an area of 0.1125 acres. By allowing the 2nd amendment petition dated 15-7-86, the trial Court allowed the plaintiff to increase the area of his dispossessed land from 0.01-1/4 acres to 0.03 acres and to change the valuation of the suit. By way of amendment for the 3rd time the plaintiff in fact and in substance sought to show his purchased land to be 0.1125 acres. Thus Mr Pal has rightly pointed out that there was no necessity of allowing such amendment to resolve the real dispute as to whether the defendant has dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land, which the plaintiff by way of 2nd amendment of the plaint claims to be 0.03 acres out of his purchased land. 

 10. In the instant suit the real dispute to be resolved by the court is as to whether the defendant has dispossessed the plaintiff from 0.03 acres of land, which has been described as the suit land in the plaint. It is not a suit for declaration of plaintiff’s title to the entire land what is covered by his kabala. It also appears from the successive petitions for amendment of the plaint that the plaintiff sought to improve his case by stages, first to meet the defendant's objection of mentioning plot No.936 and then to fit in with the report of the advocate commissioner as to the area, covered by the disputed structures of the defendant and finally, to bring a new case that he, in fact, purchased 0.1125 acres although his kabala shows the area of this purchased land to be 0.08-1/4 acres and though he claims 0.0932 acres on the boundary given in the kabala.

parties:
Ganaprojatantri Bangladesh Sarker represented by the DC, Bakergonj ----- Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Joinal Abedin Dewan & others -----  Plaintiff-Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 153 of 1978 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal for declaration of title to the suit land on the averments; inter alia, that Babar Ali as original owner of 4.16 acres of land of CS Plot Nos. 179, 180, 811, 218, 1773 and 1853 of CS Khebat No. 54 of Mouza Char Akaria in Nim Howla right, that Babar Ali leased out the land of CS Plot Nos.1773 and 1853 and the land of the remaining 4 CS Plots measuring 3.77 acres was in his khas possession, that it was recorded as RS Plot Nos. 183. 202 and 205 of RS khatian No. 226 measuring an area of 3.78 acres which is the disputed land, that one Azim Sharip and others were the superior landlords of the CS khebats in Howla right, that the khas land of Babar Ali as stated above was diluviated by the river Lata in 1344-45 BS and reformed in situ within 7/8 years next, that Babar Ali died leaving a daughter Ulfatunnessa who possessed the disputed land by payment of rent that it transpires that the disputed land has been wrongly recorded in the names of the heirs and successive heirs of the superior landlords, defendant Nos. 1-51, 53, that the defendants have no title and possession in the disputed land, that Ulfatunnessa died leaving the plaintiff as her only heir, that he has been possessing the disputed land by payment of rent, that the plaintiff asked the defendants to rectify the ROR but they refused to do so in the last part of Magh 1384 BS which has clouded the title of the plaintiff and hence the suit. 

 3. Defendant No. 52 the Government--appellant contested the suit by filing a written statement raising several objections. The case of the appellant, briefly, is that 0.63 acre of land out of the suit land has been recorded as diluviated since 1344 BS by the river Lata in SA Khatian No. 1, that the same reformed in situ after long 20 years which is the khas land of the Government, that remaining 3.15 acres land has been recorded in SA Khatian No. 1074 in the name of the Mutwalli of the Waqf Estate and that the plaintiff has acquired no title on the basis of the illegal and collusive document from the superior landlords. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge by hi judgment and decree dated 29.7.1980 dismissed the suit upon holding, among others, that the disputed land remained diluviated for more than 20 years and under the provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest of the original owner Babar Ali in the disputed land was extinguished and the same vested in the Government and, as such, the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the disputed land. 

 5. On appeal by the plaintiff from the said decree, Title Appeal No. 207 of 1980, the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Bakergonj dismissed the same by his judgment and decree dated 30.3.1982. In concurring with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the learned Additional District Judge, inter alia, found that the SA Khatian shows that the disputed land was lost to the river Lata since 1344 BS and as soon as it re-appeared, the Waqf Estate in view of the provision of President's Order No. 135 of 1972, cannot lay any claim to it and that the anxiety of the plaintiff to pay rent after the institution of the suit in the name of the Waqf Estate shows that the suit land re-appeared in the recent past. 

 86 (1) (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successor-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. 

 13. The learned Assistant Judge disbelieved the plaintiff's case and observed that the disputed land remained diluviated for more than 20 years, that it was so till SA operation and thus under the provision of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest of the original owner Babar Ali was extinguished and the disputed land had vested in the Government.

parties:
Madina Vegetable and Oil Refinery Industries (Private) Limited  -------- Plaintiff.
Vs.
M T Dolores  -------- Defendants.
full_judgment:
"The High Court of Admiralty shall have jurisdiction over any claim by the owner or consignee or assignee of any bill of lading of any goods carried into any port in England or Wales in any ship, for damage done to the goods or any part thereof by the negligence or misconduct of or for any breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, master, or crew of the ship unless it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that at the time of the institution of the cause any owner or part owner of the ship is domiciled in England or Wales: Provided always that if in any such cause the plaintiff do not recover twenty pounds he shall not be entitled to any costs, charges, or expenses incurred by him therein, unless the judges shall certify that cause was fit one to be tried in the said Court". 

 He put a great stress on the expression "bill of lading" as employed in section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 to contend that "bill of lading" means original bill of lading, a document of title to the property of the cargo and he who holds such original bills of lading the property of the cargo or the goods shipped on board of the vessel passed to him and unless and until the original bills of lading at load ports arc surrendered neither the owner of the vessel nor its master or the local agent is legally bound to issue the delivery order. He submits that in order to invoke section 6 of the Act the statement made in the plaint must disclose damage done to the goods or any part thereof or it must disclose any breach of contract on the part of the owner, master or crew of the ship. From the averments made in this plaint, he submits that plaintiff's case rests on the refusal to pass delivery order for the cargo by the defendant 5 and as the plaintiff failed the defendants 1 and 7 legally refused to issue the delivery order. Mr. Hafizullah, secondly, contends that the statements made in the plaint do not disclose that there is any breach of contract within the meaning of section 6 of the Act. He submits that as there is no cause of action for the suit either on the ground of damage done to the goods or any part thereof by the negligence or misconduct or for any breach of duty or breach of contract the Admiralty Court is not invested with jurisdiction under section 6 of the Act, and the order of arrest was passed upon an illegal assumption of jurisdiction. Thirdly, he contends that in this case as there are conflicting claims over the cargo the ship owner or the Master of the ship cannot issue delivery order for the cargo. 

 6. The Madina Vegetable and Oil Refinery Industries Limited is the plaintiff. This suit is against the principal defendant 1 'MT Dolores', a sea going vessel with Norwegian flag, defendant 2 the owners and parties interested in the said vessel, defendant 3, Master of the vessel, defendant 4, Commercial Manager of the vessel, defendant 5, local agent of the defendant 1, defendant 6, owner of the Tank Terminal in which the cargo discharged in Chittagong Port, defendant 7, Ocean Wide Freight Broker and against the pro-forma defendants 8-11. The plaintiff contracted for import of 4108.23 metric tonnes of Crude Degumned Soyabean oil in bulk from any South American port to Chittagong and its banker, defendant 11 Janata Bank opened the letter of Credit in favour of the supplier, Devon Industries Sd. Bhd for US $ 17,91,845.60 through Standard Chartered Bank, Singapore Branch, Singapore and payment was available to the supplier, by a draft drawn on the plaint at sight for 100% invoice value. The shipment by steamer oil tanker was to be accompanied by the supplier's signed invoice certifying the merchandise of South American origin full set of original clean "shipped on Board" open bill of lading drawn or endorsed to the order of Janata Bank, insurance covered by openers. The plaintiff learnt that the supplier had entered into a voyage charter-party with the owner of the defendant 1, through the defendant 4. The defendant 7 is the supplier the bills of lading for the plaintiffs' cargo. The defendant 4 by its telex dated 23.6.1993 confirmed defendant 5 that the Bills of Lading were in order. The Bank of China, Singapore by its telex dated 27.5.1993 informed the defendant 11 that it had negotiated the documents for US S 17,91,845.60 under the Letter of Credit issued by defendant 11 Bank and had certified that all terms and conditions of the credit had been complied with. The defendant 5, the agent of defendant 1, 2, 4 and 7 by its letter dated June 20, 1993 informed the plaintiff that the defendant 1 tanker vessel 'MT Dolores', was to arrive at the Port of Chittagong on or about 25.5.1993 and she will take berth at River Mooring (CDSO berth) to discharge cargo and requested the plaintiff to make necessary arrangements to receive and store the cargo on arrival and to inform in which tank terminal the cargo is to be stored and on the advice of the plaintiff the cargo of Crude Degumned Soyabean Oil was discharged into the Jamuna Oil Co. Limited tank terminal at Chittagong. For taking delivery of the charge of 4048.775 metric tons stored in the said tank terminal the plaintiff requested the defendant 5 to issue a delivery order. But defendant 5 by fax informed the plaintiff that the owner/carriers instructed not to issue delivery order for entire cargo of 9,500 metric tonnes CDSO discharged into customs bonded tanks at Chittagong until/unless the original bills of lading as issued at load port are surrendered by the Charters/suppliers (Devon) to the owners. That despite the repeated demands the defendant 5 did not issue delivery order on the plea that under the instructions of defendant 4 they are unable to issue delivery order as a result the plaintiff was deprived of the valuable cargo causing substantial loss and damage to it for non-delivery of cargo valued at Taka 7,15,53,049.00 (US$ 17,91,845.60). The plaintiff stated that in these circumstances the cause of action arose within the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and it has brought this action by institution of this suit for a decree of Taka 10,50,23,103.70 value of non-delivered cargo at Taka 7,15,53,049.00 (US $ 17,91,845.60) and for damage for loss at Taka 3,34,70,054.70 against the principal defendants. 

 9. Now I proceed to hear the contentions of the learned Advocate, Dr. Kamal Hossain refers me to the statements in the plaint, the invoice at page 1, the bills of lading page 9-27, letter dated June 20, 1993 from Seacom Shipping Limited at page 30, the Telex Message dated June 23,1993 from defendant 4 to defendant 5 page 35, the import manifest to contend that the ship carried the cargo on board belonging to plaintiff who is entitled to an order of delivery of cargo from the defendant 1 or defendant 5. 

 Dr. Kamal Hossain relying upon the telex news dated June 23, 1993 from Tromoy Shipping Norway the defendant 4 to defendant 5, Seacom Shipping Limited. Chittagong put great stress on the following words appearing in the telex"    (BB) (I)   10 OFF/BS L JANATA BANK/MADINA SEEMS OK" to contend that defendant 4 found the 10 bills of lading correct. He also relied upon a letter dated June 20, 1993 from Seacom Shipping Limited (defendant 5) addressed to the plaintiff, page 30, of the list of documents to urge that the plaintiff is the owner of the cargo in question. But, Dr. Hossain contends, by a telex message defendant 5 informed the plaintiff that the owner/carriers advised them not to issue the delivery order for the entire cargo of 9,500 metric tonnes CDSO discharged into the customs bonded tanks at Chittagong until /unless the original bills of lading as issued at load ports are surrendered by the charters/suppliers (Devon) to the owner. Drawing my attention to this paper he submits that this gives rise to a cause of action for the present suit for breach of contract for non-delivery of the cargo of the plaintiff and such facts as have been stated in the plaint this court has jurisdiction to try the suit. Dr. Kamal Hossain further contends that the Janata Bank, the advisory Bank of the plaintiff holds the original bills of lading and as such the defendant 1 and defendant 5 is liable for an action in this court for not issuing the order of delivery. Dr. Hossain vigorously pleads that it is the most effective and speedy remedy for the plaintiff to secure arrest of the ship by way of security for payment of the decretal amount. He also canvasses that the plaintiff having had already spent a huge amount of Bangladeshi currency for importing the goods if the plaintiff is not allowed to take delivery of the cargo it will have adverse effect on the currency of Bangladesh. 

 and the case of Stettin (1886-1900) in ASP RMC Vol. 6, 395. Roscoe in his treatise "Admiralty Practise" in Chapter V (4th Edition) said that the claim for damage to the goods by the negligence or misconduct or for any breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, Master or crew of the ship must be made by the owner or consignee or assignee of the bill of lading of goods. The learned author has also stated that as the right to sue is confined to the owner or consignee or assignee of bill of lading of goods the breach of duty or contract must be in relation to the goods and connected with damage to them. In Stettin it was held that where by a bill of lading goods are to be delivered to a named consignee or his assignee and it is not assigned the master is not justified in delivering to the consignee without his producing the bill of lading and if he does so and the consignee has no right to the possession of the goods, the ship owner is liable to the shipper for damages for wrongful delivery. The decision in the case of Sze Hai Tong Bank Ltd Vs. Rambler Cycle Co. Limited (1959) AC 576 is also to that effect wherein it has been held that the ship owner who delivered without production of the bill of lading does so at his peril. In delivering the goods without production of the bills of lading to a person who to its knowledge was other than one entitled under the bill of lading to receive them the carrier was liable for breach of contract and for conversion. In the above quoted passage from Carver and the principle laid down in these cases I am of the opinion that where the plaintiff in an Admiralty suit fails to produce the original bill of lading the owners of the ship or the master of the vessel or the agent of the ship cannot give delivery order of the cargo and if it is so given then the carrier shall be liable for breach of contract. In view of the language employed in section 6 of the Act I am of the opinion that in order to invoke the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 two conditions are to be satisfied from the averments of the plaint, one is the damage done to the goods on board ship by negligence or misconduct of the owner, master or crews of the ship and the other, breach of contract in relation to the cargo shipped into vessel for carriage to the port of discharge. This view of mine finds support from the observation made in Al-Sayar Navigation Co. Vs. Delta International Trader Limited and others, 34 DLR 110 (AD). The relevant passage is found in paragraph 8 of the judgment. In the instant case the plaintiff is not entitled in law to have an order of delivery of the cargo from the master of the ship or for that matter from defendant 1 or from the agent defendant 5 of the owner of the ship as it failed to produce the original bills of lading. In this case before us it appears that the local agent of the owner of the ship even made a declaration under section 55 (E) of the Customs Act, 1969 and by making such declaration the agent of the defendant 1 is under legal duty to deliver the goods to the plaintiffs on production of valid documents. The defendant 5 has issued the letter not to deliver the cargo for not surrendering of the original bills of lading and that was not opposed to law. 

 11. Mr. Hafizullah drawing my attention to the bills of lading produced by the plaintiff, contends that those are not original bills of lading and as the originals are lying with different persons it gives rise to conflicting claims over the cargo and the shipowner, Master or the crew has no liability to issue delivery order of the cargo. For this proposition of law he relies upon the following passage from Carver "Carriage by Sea' (12th Ed) Para 1041. 

 "Where there are conflicting claims the ship owner must not deliver to any but the person rightfully entitled to the goods, otherwise he may be answerable for whole value of the goods " 

 and the list of documents filed on 8th August, 1993 which includes the photo copies of the letter of the lawyer of Swiss Bank Corporation, Singapore dated August, 3,1993 accompanying the photostat copies of the original bill of lading dated 12.5.93, 14.5.93 and 19.5.93 the photostat copy of the letter of the said lawyer dated August 6, 1993 the photostat copies of telex addressed to the Tromoy Shipping, Norway (defendant No. 4) by the Northern Sales Co. Limited July 25, 1993 and the photostat copy of the letter dated 10th July, 25, 1993 and the Overseas Chinese Banking Corporation Limited ,accompanying photostat copy of the original bill of lading dated May 15,1993. The important portion for us of the letter of the 'Gabriel Peter and Partners', the lawyer of the Swiss Bank Corporation is quoted as: 

 We refer to you fax of today  Please be informed that we have 3 of the 3 original for each Bill of Lading   Again the said Solicitors on August 3 sent a Telex addressed to the Begen Ship Management As, Norway as under " 

 (II) The Bill of Lading (issued by Cranston Woodhead Agenciamento Maritime Limited as agent on behalf of the Master) dated the 19th day of May, 1993 in respect of 3,000,000 kilos Crude Degumned Soyabean Oil in Bulk to be delivered at the port of Chittagong. For your convenience we attached herewith copies of the said original Bills of Lading. Our clients now wish to present the aforesaid Bills of Lading for delivery of the goods, You are to inform when and where our clients can take delivery from your good selves. Please revert to us within seven (7) days of the date herewith failing which we will have no alternative but to proceed with all necessary steps including to protect our clients interest. The letter of OCBC Bank, 10 July, 1993 is as: 

 We hereby put you on notice that the full set of original of the above Tanker Bills of Lading is in our possession. Accordingly you  are not to release the cargo compromised in the said Tanker Bill of Lading to anyone. 

 From a close examination of the copy of the bills of lading as referred to above it appears that in the ship 'MT Dolores' Crude Degumned Soyabean Oil in Bulk stowed into tank No. PE2P, PR2S PR3P, 5S, 6C, 7P, 7C and 7S which correspond with the number of tank is shown in the bills of lading produced by the plaintiff. As I already said that the bills of lading produced by the plaintiff are not original and from the photo copies of the original bills of lading sent by OCBC Bank, Singapore it appears that they are in possession of the original and the other parties are also in possession of the original bills of lading (vide letter of Gabriel Peter and Partners). Thus in view of the commentary of Carver and the decision as quoted above the plaintiff is not entitled to the delivery order and there is no breach of contract giving rise to any cause of action for this suit. 

 12. Dr. Kamal further contends that the Janata Bank, the advisory Bank of the plaintiff, holds the original bills of lading and as such the defendant 1 and defendant 5 are liable for an action in court for breach of contract for non delivery of the cargo. Mr. Hafizullah in reply refers me to an unreported decision dated 26.6.1992 in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 145 of 1991 to contend that unless the bill of lading is retired from the Bank the owner of the cargo is not entitled to delivery order as by holding the original bills of lading title to the cargo passes to the holder of the original bills of lading. He also submits that although import manifest states the necessary particulars of the cargo shipped in the vessel showing that the plaintiff has shipped the cargo but mere issuance of import manifest does not confer the right to obtain delivery order as contended by Dr. Kamal Hossain.

parties:
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh, Dhaka ----- Defendant Appellant (in all the appeals)
Vs.
Uttar Jamalgarh Matsajibi Samabaya Samity Limited, represented by its Secretary and others Respondent ----- Plaintiff in all the appeals)
full_judgment:
2. The matter had originated from Title Suit No. 51 of 1982 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Sunamganj, which was filed by respondents Nos. 2 and 3 (plaintiffs) against respondent No. 1 (defendant No. 1)--Uttar Jamalgarh Matsya Jibi Samabaya Samity. The appellant -Government of Bangladesh, was defendant No. 4, Director of Fisheries and District Fishery Corporation were respectively defendants Nos. 2 and 3 in that suit. The Government-defendant, by a deed of lease dated 15 September 1981, leased out a fishery known as 'Bogiyani Group Fishery' to the plaintiffs-respondents for three years from 1389 B.S. to 1391 B.S. with a provision for renewal for the next three years that is, up to 1394 B.S. with a provision for renewal for the next three years, that is, upto 1394 B.S. While the plaintiffs were in possession of the fishery under the said lease, the Director of Fisheries (defendant No. 2), by an order dated 5 October 1981, leased out the said fishery to respondent defendant No. 1 for the same period, more or less; that is why the plaintiffs filed the suit praying, among other things for a declaration of nullity of the defendants' subsequent lease order dated 5 October 1981 in favour of defendant No. 1. The Government (defendant No. 4) and the subsequent lessee, defendant No. 1, contested the suit; but it was decreed by the Subordinate Judge by a judgment dated 31 August 1983. By this decree the plaintiffs lease upto 1391 B.S. was held valid and that he would also get renewal of the lease for the next three years, from 1392 to 1394 B.S. I Plaintiffs' further prayer for permanent injunction was, however, refused. 

 3. This decree was challenged by both parties in Title Appeals Nos. 259 and 269 of 1983. These appeals were disposed of by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet, by a judgment and decree dated 13 December 1983. By this appellate decree, the trial Court's decree was modified to the extent that plaintiffs' lease period was restricted to the original period of three years, that is, upto 1391 B.S. and their prayer for renewal was rejected as being 'premature'.

parties:
Halima Bibi------- Petitioner.
Vs.
The Chairman & another ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Petitioner is an old lady and a citizen of Bangladesh. Building situated at Municipal holding No. 3, Bhitar Bari Lane, PS Kotwali, Dhaka corresponding to CS Khatian No. 2718, Plot No.134, Ward No. 4, Sheet No. 50 mouza Sahar Dhaka originally belonged to one Dhum Chand Bashak and on his death aforesaid building devolved on his heirs namely Sakuntala Bashak (widow), Shantash Chandra Bashak (son) and Kani Lal Bashak (son). The heirs of Dhum Chand Bhasak sold the aforesaid building to one Hari Ballab Bashak by a registered sale-deed No. 1740 dated 18.4.1945. Original sale deed is annexed and marked as Annexure 'A' to the petition. 

 4. Hari Ballab having possessed the sale property for more than seven years, transferred the same in favour of one Pire Mohammad by registered deed of perpetual lease No. 10172 dated 21.11.1952 which was again followed by a perpetual lease on 20.1.1960. Photostat copy of the original perpetual lease deed is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'B' to the Petition. 

 5. Thereafter Pire Mohammad transferred the said property having possessed for more than eight years to one Syed Musaheb Ali by registered deed of perpetual lease No. 1930 dated 20.1.1960. Photostat copy of said original deed of perpetual lease is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'C' to the petition. After purchase of the same property Syed Mosaheb Ali mutated his name in the Revenue Records of the Govt. and in the Municipal records as owner thereof. He also paid rents and levies. Photostat certified copies of mutated SA Khatian and Municipal Tax-receipt arc annexed hereto and marked as Annexure D1 and E respectively. 

 6. The family of Syed Musaheb Ali is bilingual and they migrated from Calcutta in 1947 and settled at Patharkhola, Pabna. Later on he came and started living at Dhaka since 1960 and he was all along present in Bangladesh and his whereabouts were not unknown and he did not cease to occupy, supervise and manage the property in person till he sold the same to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and as such the property was never abandoned in any sense of the term as defined in section 21 of PO 16 of 1972. Mosaheb Ali lived and died in this country. During the war of liberation beginning from 25th March up to 16th of December, 1971 he was in possession of the said property as its lawful owner and continued to possess the same after liberation of Bangladesh till be transferred the said property to the petitioner Halima Bibi by registered sale deed No. 5147 dated 12.2.74. Original sale deed is annexed and marked as Annexure F to the petition. 

 8. Petitioner while in lawful and peaceful possession of the said property was suddenly evicted there from on 7.8.75 by Officer of the Respondent No. 2 without any prior notice and without giving her chance to show cause as to why the property should not be treated to be abandoned and to defend and to prove her lawful title in the said property. Against this said illegal and arbitrary act of eviction petitioner made several representations and prayed for release of the property in her favour and the office of the Respondent No. 2 made several correspondence with petitioner asking her to produce original title deeds in respect of the said property and to furnish information as to the place of birth and home address of Syed Musaheb Ali. 

 10. Meanwhile, Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 came into force which provided for final publication of the list of abandoned property. Accordingly list KA was published mentioning therein the building of the petitioner as abandoned property. The said law also provided for constitution of the Court of settlement of exclusion of the property from the abandoned list or restoration of the building on the ground that the building is not an abandoned property and vested in the Government under PO 16 of 1972. After the constitution of the Court of Settlement, the petitioner filed an application before the same for exclusion of her property from the abandoned list and restoration of the possession thereof on the ground that her building is not abandoned property and the same as neither vested in the Government nor her title being affected by the provision of PO 16 of 1972 stating that her vendor Mosaheb Ali was the Bangladeshi citizen and in peaceful possession of the building in question from his purchaser on 2.1.1960 till he sold the same to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and during the period of war of liberation beginning from 25th March to 16th December, 1971 Syed Mosaheb Ali neither abandoned the said property nor left the country, rather he was in peaceful possession therein. In support of her claim petitioner filed all necessary papers which included Annexure A to O to this petition before the Court of Settlement. 

 14. According to the definition 'abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh. It implies that there should be some information to the Govt. that the owner is outside Bangladesh but sub-clause II (a) further conveys the idea mere absence from Bangladesh will not render the property abandoned unless the activity of the owner of the property outside Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of the country. In other words the owner in the opinion of the Government by indulging in activity prejudicial to the interest of the State. Sub-clause 11 (a) of clause 1 of Article 2 is to be read with clause 1 of Article 2. In the case of M/s Speed Bird Navigation Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 170, their Lordships have expounded this provision of law holding that the clause referred above appears to be that the properties of those absentee owners about whose purpose of staying outside the country the Government has not yet formed any opinion whatsoever cannot be also regarded as abandoned properties, but the properties of those persons about whose purpose of staying abroad the Government has formed an adverse opinion, shall be deemed to be abandoned properties. This decision of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division which has been reported in 30 DLR (AD) page 101 and in that decision of their Lordships of the Appellate Division confirmed the view taken by their Lordships of the High Court Division and further held that the power regarding the formation of the opinion cannot be delegated to other Government officials. Their Lordships further held that" there cannot be any vesting of absentee owners of properties in the government unless there is Government's opinion expressed to the effect that his absence from the country is detrimental to the interest of the State."This definition clause is to be read as a whole in the light of the title and the preamble and also as an integral part of the Presidential Order. 

 20. The learned Advocate appearing for the 	petitioner has submitted that as per clause 3 of Article 7 of the Order, a person in occupation of abandoned properly if sought to be evicted there from is entitled to show cause notice or period i.e. 7 days within the service of notice and if he failed to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Officer shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed. 

 21. Thus it is evident that as per clause 3 of Article 7 of the Order petitioner before being evicted is entitled 10 show cause notice. But in the instant case no such notice was served. The petitioner was evicted there from though she did have valid title thereto inasmuch as Syed Mosaheb Ali who is the owner of the properly transferred it by executing and registering a sate deed Ext. F on receiving valuable consideration.

parties:
Jogesh Chandra Pal ----- Petitioner
Vs. 
Ershad Hossain Choudhury & others ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, was that Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari was the original owner of the suit premises and the defendant was a monthly tenant under her at a monthly rent of Tk. 37.00. While the tenant had been possessing the suit premises running a cloth business under the name and style "Bibekananda Store" Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari executed a deed of power of attorney and exchanged the suit premises along with other properties with one Abdul Khaleque, a migrant from India. Before regularisation of exchange the suit premises was declared as enemy property and the defendant and other persons took lease of the same from the Assistant Custodian Enemy Property, Comilla. After the regularisation of the exchange of Abdul Khaleque the suit premises was released from the list of enemy property by the Assistant Custodian by a deed of transfer. Abdul Khaleque after becoming owner transferred the suit premises along with other properties to Shafiqur Rahman and others by registered sale deed dated 22.8.73 and Shafiqur Rahman and others in their turn transferred the same to the plaintiffs by a registered sale deed dated 8.7.75. The plaintiffs thus becoming the owner of the suit premises intimated the defendant about their purchase and claimed rent from him but the defendant did not pay any heed to it. Thereafter the plaintiffs sent a notice under section 106 of the TP Act to the defendant to quit the premises and thereby the tenancy was determined. Instead of vacating the suit premises the defendant sent a reply in which the title of the plaintiff was questioned. 

 4. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit premises and the defendant petitioner is not a monthly tenant under him and no relationship of landlord and tenant does exist between the defendant and the plaintiff. It was stated by the defendant that under the Thakur Proshad Tewary Estate there were certain vacant land in Comilla town recorded in Khas khatian No. 1 in the name of the Estate owned and possessed by Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari in Taluki right. Buildings were constructed and structures were raised by different persons on the said land with the permission of the landlord to carry on business as monthly tenants under the said Estate and the defendant-petitioner paid monthly rents in the Comilla Thakur Proshad Tewary Estate obtaining rent receipts. One Baikunta Chandra Paul, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-petitioner made constructions on the lands and started business therein under the name and style "Bibekananda Store" since 1332 BS. Baikunta Chandra Paul died in 1359 leaving Arjun Chandra Paul and Narendra Chandra Paul as his brother's son. Thereafter defendant-petitioner by way of inheritance from Arjun Chandra Paul and by way of purchase of the share of Narendra Chandra Paul has been carrying on business in the premises. It was also stated that the alleged power of attorney is forged and for that matter the subsequent transfers of the shops of the suit premises in the name of Shafiqur Rahman and thereafter in the name of the plaintiffs are all sham transactions. It was alleged that Abdus Sabur Khan, a Tahshildar of the enemy property office by exerting his influence created forged Power of Attorney in the name of Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari in favour of Abdul Khaleque, a fictitious name, and created a sale deed in the name of his brother Shafiqur Rahman and other relations and then transferred the property to the plaintiffs and others. The Government having come to know about these underhand deals started criminal cases against Abdus Sabur Khan and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and others and those cases are pending for disposal. The Government having acquired the estate of Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari has virtually become the owner of the premises but has not been realising rent because of the said anti-corruption cases. The defendant instituted inter pleader suit No. 325 of 1986 for determination as to who is the real owner and the Government also contested the suit but the said was unfortunately dismissed on 15.11.88. 

 6. From the case as given out in the plaint, written statement and the evidence of witnesses of the respective parties it appears that there is no dispute with regard to the case of the plaintiff that the suit premises originally belonged to Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari and the defendant-petitioner's predecessors were monthly tenant under her on payment of rent. Admittedly the defendant did not pay rent of the suit premises since 1947. It is also not denied that the plaintiffs claimed the tenancy right in respect of the suit premises against the defendant by way of giving him the intimation of this acquisition of interest in the same and a notice under section 106 of the TP Act sent by the plaintiffs having been received, the defendant gave reply. In the reply the defendant denied the existence of relationship between him and the plaintiffs and also questioned the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in the suit premises. 

 (2) Are the plaintiffs entitled to the reliefs claimed in the suit according to the prayer made in the plaint? 

 The plaintiff's case was that as the defendant was a tenant of the suit premises under Rani Ragu Bansha Dulari and the right, title and interest of the said owner having subsequently devolved on the plaintiff the relationship which the original owners had with the defendant also devolved upon the plaintiff on his acquisition of interest over the properties with all its rights and liabilities It was further stated that as the relationship of landlord and tenant subsists between the plaintiff and the defendant, the defendant is under obligation to pay rent to the plaintiff and, in default, he is liable to be evicted under due process of law from the suit premises. It was further stated that the defendant having only a tenancy right is estopped under section 116 of the Evidence Act from challenging the title of the plaintiff who is his landlord. From the defendant's side it was not denied that his predecessor-in-interest was tenant under the original owner Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari. But the existence of relationship of landlord and tenant between the defendant and the plaintiff in respect of the suit premises were very much denied stating that neither the defendant nor his predecessor was inducted in the premises by the plaintiff or his predecessors, the alleged transferees from Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari. The defendant also never admitted the plaintiff as his landlord by way of attornment or in any other manner. The defendant petitioner also challenged the very tide of the plaintiff stating that the SCC Court has no jurisdiction to entertain and decide the suit as complicated question of title is involved. Instead of returning the plaint on the ground of maintainability, the learned SCC Judge assumed jurisdiction to try the suit and thus found that the plaintiff has become owner of the suit premises as he derived his title through Abdul Khaleque who, in turn, became owner of the suit property by way of deed of exchange which was regularised by the Government through different process. The SCC Judge also found that the defendant having claimed only the tenancy right under the original owner and having not claimed title independently to that of the plaintiff, has no right to challenge the tittle of the plaintiff. It was further held that the defendant being a tenant in respect of the suit premises under the original owner has remained a tenant under the plaintiffs who have acquired right, title and interest in the suit premises and the defendant being a defaults has rendered himself liable to be evicted from the same. 

 8. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the learned SCC Judge has committed error of law: Firstly, for not returning the plaint under section 23 of the SCC Act on the ground that the suit is not maintainable as complicated question of title is involved in the suit. Secondly, for not framing an issue as to whether there exists any relationship of landlord and tenant between the contesting parties though the said question has seriously been agitated by the defendant in the written statement. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that without framing an issue and arriving at a finding as regards the relationship of the landlord and tenant the question of default in payment of rent to the plaintiffs could not arise. With regard to the point relating to maintainability let us have a look at the provision of section 23 of Small Causes Courts Act, 1887 which reads as follows: 

 "Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this act, when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a court of small causes depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to immoveable property or other title which such a court cannot finally determine the court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a court having jurisdiction to determine the title." 

 The section thus provides that if the reliefs claimed depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to the immoveable property or other title and the court is unable to determine such title finally it may return the plaint to be presented to the proper court having jurisdiction. So it is not incumbent on the court to return the plaint in all cases and whenever and in whatever manner the question of title is raised. The court may refuse to try the suit and return the plaint only when the relief claimed is dependent on the proof or disproof of complicated question of title. The provision of section 23 of the Act does not impose upon the court an absolute bar and if it is found that the points involved can be determined by way of dealing with it incidentally the court is left 'with the discretion to try the suit. In the present suit the plaintiffs has claimed ownership over the suit premises and the defendant has not claimed any right, title and interest over the same but only claimed the tenancy right. Thus the question of title is not in controversy by the claim and counter-claim of title of the parties so as to take the suit out of the jurisdiction of Small Causes Court. Only duty cast upon the SCC Judge was to determine whether the relationship of landlord and tenant created at the time of original owner continued and existed even at the time of filing this suit and for determination of such question the SCC Judge was quite competent to deal with and determine the question of title incidentally, if it was considered necessary. In support of his contention that the SCC Judge should have returned the plaint in a suit where question of title is involved Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, referred to the case of Meraj Uddin Ahmed Vs. Anwarul Islam and another reported in 26 DLR 314 wherein it is held: 

 "Small Cause Court Judge, in case of question of title of property involved, may return the plaint, or it may not do so and try the case touching the question of title incidentally but not finally". 

 This principle is not applicable in all cases and, therefore, in the said case it has further been held: "The suit being one between alleged landlord and alleged tenant for an enforcement of certain rights of a landlord the simple question which is to be tried in such a suit is whether there is existence of any relationship of landlord and tenant. In such a case the question of title is not relevant at all". 

 "In a Small Causes Court suit between a landlord and a, tenant, the court has no power to go into the question of title except incidentally for the purpose of deciding the question raised in the suit which is absolutely necessary for decision of the case," and it is further held: 

 "A tenant inducted by the plaintiff landlord cannot deny the title of the landlord during the continuance of tenancy". 

 Thus from the reading of section 23 of the SCC Act and the principle laid down in a number of judicial pronouncements it becomes clear that the determination of the question of title is discretionary and the SCC Court has the power to decide the question of title incidentally in a suit, which is essentially of Small Cause nature and the court chooses not to return the plaint. Hence I am of the view that if the relationship of landlord and tenant is proved in favour of the landlord, the landlord's claim cannot be resisted whatever may be the state 01 things regarding the title of the property. On the other hand, if the landlord fails to establish the relationship as alleged by him he can not succeed in such a suit, even if he proves title to the property. The question of title is beyond the scope of such litigation. 

 9. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia next submits that the determination of the question of relationship of the landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendants was vital as it is asserted by the plaintiff but denied by the defendants and for that matter the SCC Court committed error of law in not framing a specific issue of the point for determination. As the derivative title of the plaintiff has been challenged the framing of such issue for determination of the above question was essential and, therefore, the learned Advocate submits that non framing of such a specific issue for the purpose of consideration and determination has caused prejudice to the petitioner. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to the case of Atauddin Mia and others Vs. Abdul Latif reported in 9 DLR 357 relevant page 361 wherein a Single Bench of this court held: 

 10. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, then submits that though the defendant was a tenant under the original owner in respect of the premises the plaintiffs have not been accepted as landlord by any agreement or by way of payment of rent or by attainment, right of landlord has not accrued on the plaintiffs, though the plaintiffs have alleged that they have acquired derivative title over the suit premises by successive transfers and for that matter the law of estoppel under section 116 of the Evidence Act has no manner of application as no relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the defendant has been established either by way of attornment or otherwise. On the other hand, Mr. Karim argues that the tenancy of the defendant in respect of the suit premises existed with Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari having not been determined by any act either from the side of the original owner or her successors or from the side of the tenant it will be deemed that the tenancy has been continuing and the plaintiffs have ownership over the suit premises with all its rights and liabilities by operation of law. The learned Advocate for the opposite party refers to the provision of section 116 of the Evidence Act which is as follows: 

 "No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant shall , during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property, and no person who came upon any immovable property by the licence of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time where such licence was given". 

 "Estoppel would operate only as regards the denial insofar as it relates to the beginning of the tenancy and not to any other point of time. Though the tenancy may be continuing jt is quite open to the tenant to plead and show that his liability to pay the rent has wholly or partially or for a time ceased as such a plea does not amount to disputing the landlord's title but is really one of confession and avoidance, and is available to the tenant". 

 It was thus the duty of the defence to show that the tenancy which was in existence with the original owner Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari was determinedly disclaimed but the defendant has not been able to prove the same therefore, it is held that the tenancy is continuing along with the suit premises and with the transfer of ownership of the suit premises the plaintiffs stepped into the shoes of the original landlord as they acquired the right over the same with all its appurtenances and privileges. 

 "It provides that neither the tenant nor anyone claiming through tenant shall be heard to deny that particular landlord had at that date title to the property, what all such persons are precluded from denying is that the lessor had title at the date of lease, there is no exception to the case where the lease itself discloses the defect to title the principle does not apply to disentitle the tenant and deny the derivative title of the person who claims to have such because entitled to the reversion though in such cases there might be estoppel i.e. attornment and acceptance of rent, etc. In the same, the principle only applies to the title of the landlord who let the tenant in as distinct from any other person claiming to be reversioner. Nor does the principle apply to prevent a tenant from pleading that the title of the original lessor has since come to an end". 

 "Whenever there is an assignment of the interest of a lessor or the interest of a lessee in a lease a new relationship comes into existence between the two sets of person one of whom was not party to the original agreement. In England at common law, an assignment was not complete without attainment by the lessee to the assignee of the original lessor, except when the assignment was by will. Later it was realised that this necessity of an attornment by the lessee was a restriction on the right of a lessor to transfer and assign his interest in a lease, and so this necessity of attornment was done away by legislative interference. This Law of Property Act, 1925, which replaced the earlier statute, has also made it clear that in such a situation, the attornment by the lessee was not necessary. In view of section 109 of the Act which says that if the lessor transfers the property leased, the- transferee in absence of a contract to contrary shall possess all the rights, and if the lessee so elects, be subject to all liabilities of the lessor as to the property so transferred, there is no requirement of attornment by the lessee. In view of this provision, the assignee of the lessor has against the lessee all the rights that he had and can enforee not only covenants but even conditions. The right to receive rent from the lessee in terms of the lease is one of such rights which passed to the assignee and a lessee cannot deny that he is not bound to pay the same as he used to pay merely because there is no privity of contract between him and the assignee who is not the landlord. The matter will be different if subsequent to the assignment, any fresh contract is entered into between the new assignees and the lesse to alter the terms of the lease, including the date of commencement of the monthly tenancy and rate of rent which will be payable". 

 12. Here in the present case there is no proof that the tenancy under the plaintiffs predecessor has come to an end, or that it has been determined by any act of the parties, or by lapse of time by operation of law and hence it cannot be said that on cessation of tenancy right the defendant-petitioner has become the absolute owner of the premises and therefore not answerable to the plaintiff or to anybody having better claim over the property so far it relates to the title in the same. The learned SCC Judge has in fact, dealt with the material questions in dispute and found to have decided the point after consideration of materials available on record. The learned SCC Judge discussed the question of title so far it was necessary for determining the points raised incidentally and not finally and therefore, no error is found to have been committed in this regard by the learned SCC Judge in his judgment. The point as to whether the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant subsisted at the time of filing of the suit and whether the defendant paid rent to the landlord has also been decided by SCC Judge on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record. The evidence shows that the defendant was admittedly tenant under the previous landlord Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari and there is nothing to show that the said tenancy came to an end by acts of the parties or by operation of law and that the defendant petitioner ever paid rents to the Government or to anybody claiming right, title and interest in the same.

parties:
Planters (Bangladesh) Ltd ------ Appellants
 Vs. 
Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd. (in liquidation) and others------ Respondents
full_judgment:
3. On 29 March, 1927 one Sarada Kripa Lala sold the suit properties to Dr. Beni Mohan Das who mortgaged them to the plaintiff-Bank on 31 March, 1927 for Tk. 75,000/- only and the latter transferred his rights, title and interest in the suit properties to Rangapani Tea Co. Ltd. Without mentioning the mortgage the transferee company and the mortgagor sold their right, title and interest in the mortgaged property to the plaintiff-Bank, on 28 August, 1935 for Tk. 1,25,000/-. The plaintiff Bank which was put in possession of the properties invested further sums of money thereon. Defendant Hill Top Tea Company Limited purchased the properties with all their Machineries for Tk. 4,00,000/-which was borrowed from the Model Bank Limited.
