The defendant company approached the plaintiff Bank for loan. One S.N. Mukherjee who was Managing Director of the defendant company and also a Director of the plaintiff Bank succeeded in obtaining the loan of Tk. 4,00,000/- from the Bank by depositing the title deeds to the Bank as a security against the loan. Under section 114 of the Companies Act, 1913 the mortgage was registered. Having failed to recover the principal or interest accruing thereon amounting to Tk. 2,40,000/- the plaintiff Bank instituted the aforesaid suit. 

 4. The Hill Top Tea Company Limited filed a written statement contending that as no consideration was passed nor any payment was made, mere depositing of title deeds did not create any mortgage. No debt, therefore, actually existed. Further, the plaintiff Bank being pressured by the Reserve Bank of India took resort to some fraudulent devices and created the defendant company to which the tea estate was sold. As a result of an understanding between the Directors of the plaintiff Bank and the defendant company and in collusion with the Directors of the Model Bank Limited, Calcutta, a cheque for TK. 4,00,000/-was drawn by it upon the Model Bank Limited, Calcutta in favour of the Mahaluxmi Bank, Calcutta. According to the defendant-company the whole transaction was only but a paper transaction and the Bank manipulated its books and accounts in order to show payment of the aforesaid sum. 

 9 In accepting the submissions made by the Counsel of the plaintiff Bank that the evidence produced on its behalf were admissible under section 65 of the Banking Companies Ordinance, section 4 of the Bankers Evidence Act. 1891 and the entries in the books of the plaintiff Bank regularly kept in course of business were relevant and also that D.P. notes, the resolution of the defendant company, Ext.3, letter Ext.3 (b), certificate under section 114 of the Companies Act, original Title deeds Exts. l and 2, passbook and the balance sheet of the defendant Company which were filed by the plaintiff-Bank, the learned Judges of the High Court Division arrived at the finding that the defendant took a loan from the plaintiff-Bank and was, therefore, liable to pay the same to the Bank. The judgment and decree passed by Abu Md. Abdullah, J. in Transferred Suit No. 8 of 1965 (arising out of Mortgage Suit No. 26 of 1960) was affirmed by the trial court. 

 9. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the defendant appellant, made strenuous efforts to prove that no loan was ever advanced by plaintiff Bank to the defendant Hill Top Tea Company Limited and what appears from the Bank's papers and entries therein and also title deeds alleged to be deposited with the plaintiff Bank were all collusive and fraudulent. There was no liability of the defendant company for the payment of the alleged loan. What appear from the papers of the plaintiff Bank were mere manipulations for the purpose of showing the loan and the mortgage deposit of title deeds. The learned Counsel particularly stressed that such manipulations were evident from the pasting in the Bank's clean cash book, Ext. 5. Apart from the legal effects of the deposit of title deeds and other relevant papers referred to above showing the advance loan to the defendant company by creating a mortgage of their property, vide, deposit of title deeds with the plaintiff Bank, which have been discussed and considered by the learned Judges of the High Court Division, they had considered at length the arguments relating to the pasting in the aforesaid Exts. This appears from their observations : 

 13. The argument that no amount was actually paid by the plaintiff Bank would seems more surprising in view of the fact that title deeds were deposited with the Bank along with all other usual documents which were executed by the predecessor of the defendant company for securing the loan amount. To this must also be added the regular entries in the ledger book and the clean cash book of the plaintiff Bank in respect of this loam in this context, the attempt to disprove the actual payment appears like trying to disprove something which is obvious and a fact that cannot be negatived by any means. To prove that no cash amount was at all paid by the plaintiff Bank for payment to the Model Bank, it was stated that, firstly, no permission was taken from the authority to transmit this amount to Calcutta which is in a different state and secondly, it was stated to have been deposited in the Model Bank on 30th June, 1948, which was a Bank holiday.

Abdus Salam & ors ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
1. This appeal is directed against an order dated 4-6-81 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Bhola in Title Suit No. 80 of 1981 allowing the plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction and restraining the defendants from dispossessing the plaintiffs from the suit land. Respondent Nos. 1 to 70, as plaintiffs, filed a suit being title suit No. 63 of 1981 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal for a simple declaration of title to Char land of Rupapura Sonapura Mouza within P.S. Bhola. The suit on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 80 of 1981 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola. The facts giving rise to the suit are the following: 

 2. The suit char-land comprising Rupapura Sonapura Mouza bearing Revenue Survey No. 1547 originally appertained to Touzi No. 1566 of Noakhali Collectorate. It was transferred to Bakerganj Collectorate in the year 1965. The Char-land was in existence from before 1860 and upto 1894 when it went into the river. It reappeared and reformed in situ in the year 1947-48. As a great number of river claimants were about to take forcible possession of the land, the Collector of Bakerganj attached it and made a reference to the Civil Court under Section 5(1) of the Bengal Alluvial Lands Act, 1920 for determination as to who were the persons having title to it. The reference, originally registered as Title Suit No. 56 of 1954 was, on transfer, renumbered as Title Suit No. 66 of 1957 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal. Government was one of the claimants. Government claimed that this Mouza Rupapura Sonapura appertained to Touzi No. 5077 of Bakerganj Collectorate. It was contended that though the original land appertained to Touzi No. 1566 of Noakhali Collectorate it was transferred to Bakerganj Collectorate in 1865 and was assigned Touzi No. 5077. For default in payment of revenue, it was purchased by Government on March 24, 1875, whereupon all subordinate interests were annulled and it was under periodical settlements with different persons till it was completely diluviated in 1894. It reappeared and reformed in situ in 1947-48. The appellants before us were claimants of Group 'B' of the reference case. Their case was that inspite of its transfer from Noakhali to Bakerganj Collectorate this mouza retained the original Touzi No. 1566 and claimants had their mirash ejara right in the mouza at a jama of Tk. 82-4-0 annas. They contended that this mouza was not auction purchased by the Government in the year 1875 and the land purchased by the Collector in auction bears Touzi No. 5077. The claimants of Group 'B' filed a suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court Barisal, being numbered as Title Suit No. 47 of 1950 of that Court. This Suit, on transfer to the local third Court of Sub ordinate Judge, was renumbered as Title Suit No. 26 of 1954. Both the reference and the suit were tried together. The trial Court decreed the Title Suit No. 66 of 1957 in favour of the Government and dismissed the Title Suit No. 26 of 1954 brought by the claimants of Group 'B'. First Appeal Nos. 119 and 120 of 1951 arose and in appeal the High Court Division accepted the contention of the claimants of Group 'B', the appellants before us and rejected and reference of the Collector. The High Court Division found that the land of the suit belonging to mouza Rupapura Sonapura bearing Revenue Survey No. 1547 appertained to Touzi No. 1566 and was not auction sold and purchased by the Collector as alleged by the Government. The High Court Division further found that government had auction purchased Touzi No. 5077 of Bakerganj Collectorate which was a Touzi different from Touzi No. 1566 originally of Noakhali Collectorate and subsequently transferred to Bakerganj Collectorate and the land of the suit did not appertain to that Touzi purchased by the Government. The Division Bench found title of the disputed land in the appellants before us and decreed their suit. Leave to appeal before the Appellate Division was refused. Thereafter the plaintiffs have brought the present suit for declaration of their title claiming title on the strength of raiyati settlements between the years 1958-1959, 1959-60 and 1960-61. The plaintiffs alleged. that the defendants-appellants and their co-sharers on suppression of facts and without affording opportunity to the Revenue Officer of the Government secured the decree in the first appeal from the High Court Division and that they being raiyats under the Government for more than 12 years Were not liable to be evicted. 

 5. Mr. Habibur Rahman the learned Advocate for the appellants has taken us through the impugned order of the learned Subordinate judge and the materials on record. The learned Advocate submits that in the first appeal Nos. 119 and 120 of 1961 before the High Court Division over the suit properties the High Court Division has found that Government had no title to them and the defendants-appellants had title thereto. The plaintiffs claimed through the Government as lessees under it. They have taken lease during the pendency of the earlier legal proceedings and were bound by the judgment and decree of the first appeals and they could not deny title of the defendants-appellants nor could they claim title in themselves. The learned Advocate further submits that after winning the cases upto the Appellate Division the defendants have applied to the Collector for getting possession in the suit land whereupon the plaintiffs have filed the present suit. The only intention of the plaintiffs is to defeat the claim of the defendants-appellants based on the decree obtained up to the Appellate Division. 

 7. We have been taken through the Plaint of the present suit. The plaint of the present suit alone is sufficient to show that the land of the present suit is identical with the land of earlier legal proceedings. Apart from it we have also gone through the Memo of Reference of the Reference Case judgment and decrees of the earlier legal proceedings. Title Suit No. 66 of 1957 (reference) and Title Suit No. 26 of 1954) and other relevant materials. It is evident that the land of the present suit is identical with the land of the earlier suits. It appears from the impugned judgment and order that an order of local investigation was obtained for identification of the land. The learned Subordinate Judge has expressed a view that it would be convenient to determine or decide the point after local investigation-but in doing so, he has ignored that the land of the earlier reference suit and the other suit are, on the showing of the plaint of the present suit itself, identical. 

 8. Apparently the land of the present suit is identical with the land of the previous suits and we see no difficulty in holding that the Government has no title in the land and the defendant appellants are owners thereof the plaintiffs who are lessees of the Government pendente lite are bound by the judgment and the decision of the previous legal proceeding. The plaintiffs cannot have a better claim of title than the Government. In the result the plaintiffs also must be found to have no title in the suit land. 

 9. We are conscious that while we are making those observations, we are touching the merit of the suit but in a case of this nature we see no other way hut to touch the merit of the suit because here is a case Where the defendant-appellants claim to resist the prayer of injunction made by the plaintiffs who are admittedly in possession on the allegation that the defendant-appellants are the owners and the plaintiffs are trespassers. In such a case, in order to See as to whether the plaintiffs have a prima facie and arguable case, it is necessary to investigate the title of the parties to some extent and.to look into the ex-facie title of the parties as we have done here. The defendant appellants have after long drawn litigation succeeded their claim and they have applied to the Collector to get possession under section 6 of the Bengal Alluvial Lands Act, 1920 which provides as follows: 

 "Whenever the Court makes an order under section 5, sub-section (2), it shall certify to the Collector its decision, and the Collector Shall thereupon put the person stated in such order to be entitled to the land in possession thereof." 

 If it is held that because the plaintiffs are in possession the defendants should not be allowed to disturb their possession till disposal of the suit the defendant-appellants are likely to take another decade to get their relief. The lands were taken possession of by the Govt. and the Govt. has leased them out to the plaintiffs. The appellants have on their case against the Govt. and in terms of section 6 of the Bengal Alluvial Lands Act they are entitled to be put into possession. In such situation the plaintiffs cannot on the strength of their possession alone, in the absence of any prima facie and arguable title, claim to restrain the defendant appellants from getting possession in accordance with law. 

 10. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury has contended that the order of the learned Subordinate Judge is merely an order of ad-interim injunction and this does not call for an interference. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has made the impugned order after hearing both the parties and considering the objection raised by the defendants. While making the order the learned Subordinate Judge has also directed the defendants to show cause within 7 days of receipt of notice as to why they should not be restrained from dispossessing the plaintiffs from the suit land. It is not understood why after considering the Objections of the defendants who had already appeared it became necessary for the learned Subordinate Judge to issue fresh notices to show cause. Be that as it may the materials that have been placed before us were admittedly placed before the learned Subordinate Judge, also and on these materials the learned Subordinate Judge has made the order of injunction be it temporary or ad-interim. Even if it is an ad-interim order of injunction, it is appealable. On consideration of the materials placed before us we have found that the plaintiffs do not appear to have any prima facie and arguable title in the suit land and the defendants are the prima fade owners of the suit land. The plaintiffs being trespassers cannot get an injunction ad-interim or temporary, against the defendants who are the owners of the suit land.
